articles.title: Trump administration planning to reimburse doctors treating vaccine ‘injury’
articles.summary: Experts warn that sweeping changes elevate health secretary RFK Jr’s anti-vaccine agenda and personal profit
articles.body:
The Trump administration is finalizing a rule to reimburse doctors who diagnose, treat and counsel patients with side effects from vaccines in what experts believe is an attempt to undermine trust in vaccines and to create an evidence base on their purported risks.

Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), also announced the creation of a vaccine "injury" research center at the National Institutes of Health and has sought to reshape the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) – actions that point to Kennedy's longtime activism against vaccination as well as the profits he and his network have made from vaccine lawsuits.

Kennedy and his allies have also profited from growing misinformation peddled through books, paid speaking events and the supplement industry.

"I do think he's a real ideologue – he really believes in this," said Dorit Reiss, professor of law at UC Law San Francisco. But Kennedy and his allies are likely "very happy to make money doing it", she said.

Peter Hotez, professor and dean of Baylor College of Medicine's National School of Tropical Medicine, agreed, saying Kennedy's actions are likely a combination of "being an ideological zealot and making money either for himself or for his associates".

Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, said the department "categorically reject claims that Secretary Kennedy is pursuing personal gain or seeking to dismantle American medicine".

Prior to his confirmation hearing in January 2025, Kennedy disclosed $2.5m in income from referrals for vaccine-related lawsuits. In the hearing, Kennedy would not commit to forgoing compensation from vaccine lawsuits after he leaves office. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, listed several ways in which Kennedy's actions, some of which have now happened, could influence future litigation.

"Kennedy can kill off access to vaccines and make millions of dollars while he does it," Warren said at the hearing. "Kids might die. But Robert Kennedy can keep cashing in." She pointed to Kennedy's involvement in litigation against Merck for its HPV vaccine – lawsuits that were settled for more than $50m in June 2026. After the confirmation hearing, Kennedy said his son would receive the money, expected to be 10% of the total; it's unclear if he did.

"For most of us, money going to our children isn't exactly money not going to us," Reiss said. "There's a dozen ways he and his family could benefit" from Kennedy's actions, she added.

Kennedy has long profited from his anti-vaccine misinformation. Tony Lyons, Kennedy's publisher and a central figure in the constellation of Maha political organizations, reportedly paid Kennedy $4m in book advances over the past year. The publisher also paid Kennedy $451,000 in consulting fees before he became HHS secretary. That's on top of other book sales and paid speaking engagements over the years. Kennedy also earned $326,000 for the 15 weeks he served as chairman of Children's Health Defense in 2023 – more than half of his $510,000 salary in 2022.

More recently, he received free flights and trips on a yacht from a former donor to his presidential campaign, who is now under investigation by the Senate for the gifts totaling some $250,000.

As HHS secretary, Kennedy has also loosened regulations on peptides, a booming part of the largely unregulated wellness industry.

"I think he's doing what everyone knew he was going to do," said Hotez. Kennedy, before and during his tenure as leader of HHS, has been "chipping away at public confidence in vaccines and immunizations in favor of products that can be sold by the wellness industry", he added.

Aaron Siri, Kennedy's former lawyer who represents people who say they have experienced severe side effects, has advocated for changing all vaccines to "shared clinical decision-making". If those changes took place, Siri could argue that the vaccines are not covered under the VICP and therefore open to litigation.

"A lot of what he is doing is geared toward setting up a more profitable litigation atmosphere," Reiss said.

Siri did not respond to the Guardian's question about profiting from litigation, but instead argued that "if vaccines are as 'safe' as touted by the government, then there should be no need for immunity to liability and, likewise, there should be very few, if any, successful cases".

The most common claim to VICP – making up more than half – has to do with where the vaccine is administered, not the vaccines themselves.

The VICP was established in 1986 in order to expedite compensation for anyone who experienced adverse side effects from vaccines. There are real costs to undermining the program, Reiss said. It's very rare for people to develop severe side effects after vaccination, but when they do, they should be compensated, she said. But if false claims about vaccine harms proliferate, they will obscure those with legitimate claims.

Filing a VICP claim is an easier process than winning a lawsuit, which takes time and effort and also demands a higher burden of proof.

"That's why the whole vaccine injury system was set up," Hotez said. "It was actually to the plaintiff's benefit to get a faster judgment without having to show detailed evidence of proof."

Without VICP, patients would need to pay lawyers a large chunk of their settlements, if their case moves through the courts at all, Reiss said: "The lack of contingency fee means they don't have to pay 30% to 50% of their earnings through the lawyer."

Compensating doctors for reporting side effects to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) risks offering "the wrong incentives" to unscrupulous providers who could increase such activities to become a new revenue source, Reiss said.

The changes could "certainly" be used by organizations such as Children's Health Defense to legitimize its work spreading misinformation "and convince donors and others that they should give them more money", she added.

VAERS, alongside several other vaccine monitoring systems, works well to pick up signals of very rare side effects, such as myocarditis from initial mRNA Covid vaccines and thrombotic thrombocytopenia in the Johnson and Johnson Covid vaccine, Hotez noted. But it's not built to prove links between vaccines and certain side effects, as vaccination opponents have attempted to do, he said.

"The VAERS system was never meant to show cause and effect," Hotez said. "It's like looking for signs of alien communication in outer space. You look at every little blip, and almost all of them have nothing, are not real. But you have to analyze them."

Years ago, Hotez engaged Kennedy in a series of conversations about misinformation that autism spectrum disorder is related to vaccines. Hotez pointed to known environmental influences on autism, like the anti-seizure medication valproic acid. Kennedy "had no interest then; he has no interest now", Hotez said. "Even back then, there was a heavy emphasis on being a plaintiff attorney and suing vaccine companies. So that's his narrow interest, which has nothing to do with reality – and he's still going by the same playbook."

Kennedy has attacked medical journals and schools, and funding for medical research has fallen sharply under his leadership. Such actions appear intended to "completely wipe out American medicine as we know it in favor of this whole system of grifting and pseudoscience", Hotez said.

articles.title: Parlamentares querem alternativa a ajuste fiscal que divide esquerda | G1
articles.standfirst: Propostas buscam alternativas à proposta do governo Lula criticada por alas da esquerda. Deputado critica condução do projeto e ataques a quem discorda das medidas.
articles.summary: Ajuste fiscal: Lindbergh Farias e partidos de esquerda propõem taxar bancos e investimentos para evitar cortes em políticas sociais e equilibrar as contas públicas.
articles.body:
O ministro do Planejamento e Orçamento, Bruno Moretti — Foto: Fabio Rodrigues Pozzebom/Agência Brasil

Lideranças de PT , PCdoB e PSOL devem apresentar ao governo alternativas ao projeto de ajuste fiscal, que enfrenta resistência de setores da esquerda, segundo o deputado federal Lindbergh Farias (PT-RJ).

As propostas estão sendo debatidas desde a semana passada por parlamentares contrários a pontos da proposta para equilibrar as contas públicas. Nesta segunda-feira (16), o vice-líder do governo no Congresso participou de uma nova reunião com lideranças parlamentares para discutir o tema.

Ao g1 , o deputado afirmou que espera uma negociação com o Executivo. “Se podem negociar com o mercado, podem negociar com a gente”, disse Lindbergh.

As medidas anunciadas pelo governo provocaram críticas de integrantes do próprio PT e reações no Congresso e nas redes sociais. A insatisfação chegou também ao canal de WhatsApp "Exército do Lula ", que teve atuação expressiva na campanha de reeleição do presidente.

O texto-base da proposta foi aprovado no Senado na semana passada, e a previsão é que entre na pauta de votações da Câmara nesta terça-feira (17).

Antes da votação, a bancada do PT na Câmara deve se reunir com o ministro do Planejamento, Bruno Moretti, para discutir o assunto.

Audiência Pública – Situação da BR-393 no trecho entre Jamapará (Sapucaia/RJ) e Volta Redonda/RJ. Dep. Lindbergh Farias (PT-RJ) — Foto: Vinicius Loures / Câmara dos Deputados

Segundo Lindbergh, as alternativas que serão apresentadas buscam preservar as políticas sociais e aumentar a contribuição de setores de maior renda para o equilíbrio das contas públicas. O governo defende que o projeto que está em votação já preserva políticas sociais.

“As medidas vão no sentido de evitar que o ajuste fiscal promova cortes em políticas sociais”, afirmou. Lindbergh disse que as propostas que deverão ser apresentadas também procuram taxar o “andar de cima”, incluindo bancos e investimentos.

O deputado criticou a condução do projeto pelo governo e afirmou que a falta de discussão prévia agravou a resistência dentro da base.

“Essa proposta do ajuste fiscal foi mal conduzida. Foi apresentada sem falar com ministros, líderes do governo, e aí depois quiseram votar em um dia só. Depois, piorou a tratativa quando tentaram desqualificar quem estava criticando a proposta”, declarou.

O ministro do Planejamento e Orçamento, Bruno Moretti, defende o pacote e afirma que as medidas não preveem redução do salário mínimo nem o fim dos pisos constitucionais de saúde e educação, pontos que vem sendo questionados pelos críticos.

No domingo (15), o vice-presidente Geraldo Alckmin disse que o projeto de ajuste fiscal do governo é uma medida tomada "na direção correta".

"O governo não mexe na população mais pobre, estão preservados ganhos de natureza social e trabalha para superávit e não ter déficit nas contas publicas. É fundamental para baixar juros. Quem mais ganha com isso é população mais pobre", disse Alckmin.

Nesta segunda-feira (16), o dólar fechou em alta de 2,15%, cotado a R$ 5,7767 . Parte do mercado financeiro considera as medidas previstas no pacote fiscal do governo insuficientes para conter o avanço da dívida pública. Alckmin, por sua vez, afirmou que não há razão para oscilações no mercado e destacou que o Brasil tem segurança jurídica .

O projeto de ajuste fiscal defendido pelo governo do presidente Lula (PT) abriu uma disputa dentro da esquerda sobre os rumos da política econômica no próximo mandato. A divergência envolve integrantes do próprio PT, parlamentares de partidos aliados e movimentos sociais que apoiaram a reeleição do presidente.

Enquanto a equipe econômica defende que as medidas são necessárias para equilibrar as contas e preservar as políticas sociais, críticos afirmam que novas restrições aos gastos podem comprometer serviços públicos e investimentos. Também questionam a falta de diálogo com a base e a velocidade da tramitação no Congresso.

A deputada Erika Hilton (PSOL-SP) e a deputada federal eleita Ana Elisa (PT-MG) são dois dos nomes entre os que criticaram a proposta do governo.

“É inaceitável que a Faria Lima exija que o governo Lula coloque em prática os planos de governo de Flávio Bolsonaro. [...] A responsabilidade fiscal é importante, mas isso não é um argumento válido pra sucatear a vida das pessoas", afirmou Erika em publicação no X.

A discussão ganhou força após o ministro do Planejamento, Bruno Moretti, afirmar, em entrevista ao jornal "Folha de S.Paulo" publicada no domingo (15), que uma parcela “sectária” da esquerda atrasa o combate a privilégios ao se opor ao projeto. Segundo o ministro, essa resistência beneficia setores que tentam escapar do ajuste.

O deputado André Janones (Rede-MG), responsável pelo canal “Exército do Lula” no WhatsApp, também reagiu às críticas. Em uma mensagem, afirmou que o movimento contra o ajuste “não tem nada de orgânico” e “está sendo direcionado por um bando de radicais”.

“E não deixamos de ser reféns da extrema direita pra ser refém desses pseudo-revolucionários de apartamento que nunca fizeram porra nenhuma pelo país”, escreveu Janones no "Exército do Lula".

A insatisfação também apareceu no canal: seguidores passaram a usar o emoji de tesoura nas reações às publicações de Janones, em alusão à contenção de gastos prevista no pacote. Apesar das divergências entre parlamentares petistas, a direção nacional do PT declarou apoio às medidas encaminhadas ao Congresso.

Questionado pela reportagem sobre as declarações de Janones, Lindbergh afirmou que é amigo do deputado e que deve procurar o mineiro para uma conversa. O petista defendeu seu direito de criticar as medidas e disse que sua intenção é contribuir para que o governo dê certo.

Para Lindbergh, o mercado financeiro está “tentando levar o governo Lula a uma recessão". O parlamentar afirmou que sua preocupação é com os efeitos do ajuste em um cenário de desaceleração econômica.

Entre os críticos do ajuste também está o deputado federal eleito Jones Manoel (PSOL-PE), que argumenta que o endurecimento das regras fiscais pode comprometer políticas públicas. Nesta segunda-feira, ele afirmou ao UOL que foi colocado em uma disputa com Janones que não procurou.

A pergunta foi feita ao deputado eleito depois que Jones publicou um vídeo em seu canal no Youtube em que afirmou que "influencers governistas" estariam acusando críticos a proposta de serem "pautados pela mídia burguesa". "Começaram a me atacar dizendo que espalhei fake news".

Ao comentar as críticas ao PLP 299/2026, o deputado eleito Jones Manoel (PSOL-PE) disse que o embate foi alimentado nas redes e afirmou não ter relação pessoal com Janones, apesar de já ter participado de eventos com ele. Os dois passarão a conviver como congressistas da mesma federação partidária.

“Eu não critiquei em momento nenhum o André Janones. Ele fez um direcionamento de que as pessoas que estavam criticando o PLP eram mentirosos, eram a esquerda radical, a extrema esquerda. E as pessoas criaram uma polarização, Jones Manoel versus André Janones. Mas eu em momento nenhum citei o nome do deputado. Eu estou totalmente inocente nessa história, de uma disputa que eu não quero, que eu recuso e que eu não procurei em relação ao Janones”, disse.

O projeto reúne restrições ao crescimento das despesas federais, mudanças no cálculo do piso da saúde e redução de benefícios tributários para empresas. O pacote anunciado pelo governo também inclui medidas contra supersalários no funcionalismo.

Entre as mudanças está a possibilidade de limitar, em determinadas condições, o crescimento das despesas acima da inflação a 2%, abaixo do teto de 2,5% previsto no arcabouço fiscal. A proposta também amplia os mecanismos de bloqueio de recursos durante a execução do Orçamento.

O texto-base foi aprovado pelo Senado na quinta-feira (12), por 45 votos a 31, mas ainda depende da votação dos destaques, prevista para esta terça-feira (17), antes de seguir à Câmara. O governo afirma que as medidas buscam equilibrar as contas e conter o avanço da dívida pública.

A reação ao pacote também chegou à mobilização nas ruas. A UNE (União Nacional dos Estudantes) convocou atos em ao menos dez cidades para terça-feira (17), contra o ajuste fiscal.

A organização do protesto foi criticada nas redes sociais. Em uma publicação na página da UNE no Instagram, perfis dizem que os atos contra o ajuste fiscal podem prejudicar o governo Lula e alimentando críticas de movimentos da Direita.

A presidente da UNE, Beatriz Borges, diz que é importante ressaltar que os atos não são contra o governo eleito. "Estamos indo contra o mercado que mesmo tendo seu projeto econômico derrotado nas eleições, quer impor a sua vontade", em alusão ao plano de governo do candidato derrotado Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

"Nosso objetivo é alterar profundamente o PLP, retirando os mecanismos que aprofundam a austeridade e limitam a capacidade do Estado de investir no desenvolvimento do país. Reconhecemos que existem medidas positivas, como a determinação de enfrentamento da questão dos supersalários pelo Congresso Nacional e a revisão de benefícios fiscais. Não somos contra essas iniciativas. Mas não podemos aceitar os pontos do projeto que aprofundam a austeridade e limitam a capacidade do Estado de investir no povo", afirma.

Questionada sobre os próximos passos caso o governo mantenha a proposta, Beatriz afirmou que a entidade acompanhará a tramitação, dialogará com parlamentares e seguirá mobilizando estudantes em todo o país.

“Queremos que o Congresso retire os dispositivos que aprofundam a austeridade e que o governo assuma o compromisso de ampliar os investimentos públicos”, disse.

articles.title: Paulo Gomes (PL) será líder do governo de Sergio Moro na Alep | G1
articles.standfirst: O líder do governo na Alep é o deputado estadual escolhido pelo governador para ser o porta-voz e interlocutor do Poder Executivo dentro da Casa Legislativa.
articles.summary: O líder do governo na Alep é o deputado estadual escolhido pelo governador para ser o porta-voz e interlocutor do Poder Executivo dentro da Casa Legislativa.
articles.body:
Paulo Gomes será líder do governo de Sergio Moro na Assembleia Legislativa do Paraná — Foto: Orlando Kissner

O deputado estadual Paulo Gomes ( PL ) será o líder do governo Sergio Moro na Assembleia Legislativa do Paraná (Alep), a partir de 2027. A informação foi confirmada ao g1 nesta segunda-feira (16) pela equipe do governador eleito.

➡️ O líder do governo na Alep é o deputado estadual escolhido pelo governador para ser o porta-voz e interlocutor do Poder Executivo dentro da Casa Legislativa. Em geral, ele defende os interesses e as posições do Executivo, mobiliza e organiza os deputados da base de apoio e indica em plenário como a bancada governista deve votar em relação às pautas em discussão.

"Agradeço imensamente pela confiança depositada em mim para desempenhar uma missão tão importante para o futuro do nosso estado. Ser líder do governo é assumir o compromisso de construir pontes entre os Poderes Executivo e Legislativo, promover o diálogo, buscar o entendimento entre os parlamentares e contribuir para que projetos e propostas que beneficiem a população paranaense avancem com responsabilidade, transparência e eficiência. Sei da importância e dos desafios dessa missão", afirmou o deputado.

Paulo Gomes tem 55 anos e é advogado desde 1994. Aos 23 anos, ingressou na Procuradoria do Estado por concurso público. Ele é especialista em Código de Defesa do Consumidor e também atua como apresentador de um programa de televisão.

Gomes foi eleito deputado estadual pela primeira vez em 2022 pelo Progressistas (PP) e reeleito em 2026 pelo Partido Liberal (PL). A partir de 2027, a bancada do partido na Alep contará com 14 deputados, incluindo Gomes .

articles.title: PF cita 'quebra de confiança' para afastamento de delegados e nega interferência em investigação | G1
articles.standfirst: Os delegados da PF afastados de suas funções, participaram da elaboração de relatórios sobre o envolvimento de ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal com o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro.
articles.summary: Os delegados da PF afastados de suas funções, participaram da elaboração de relatórios sobre o envolvimento de ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal com o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro.
articles.body:
Em resposta ao Ministério da Justiça, o diretor-geral da Polícia Federal (PF), Andrei Rodrigues, afirmou que houve uma "quebra na fundamental relação de confiança" ao falar sobre o afastamento de dois delegados de suas funções na coordenadoria-geral de repressão à corrupção, crimes financeiros e lavagem de dinheiro e negou interferência na investigação sobre o Master .

"Em razão de critérios de conveniência e oportunidade administrativa, tendo em vista que a dinâmica de fatos recentes demonstrou que houve uma quebra na fundamental relação de confiança mútua que deve existir entre as funções de chefia direta e hierarquicamente relacionadas, optou-se por não se dar prosseguimento ao processo que designava os servidores Daniel Mostardeiro Cola e Wedson Cajé Lopes para as novas funções de confiança criadas".

Os delegados da PF afastados de suas funções, participaram da elaboração de relatórios sobre o envolvimento de ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) com o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro.

Os relatórios reuniam menções a três ministros da Corte: Alexandre de Moraes, Dias Toffoli e Kassio Nunes Marques.

A direção-geral da PF determinou que o material seja refeito . A cúpula da corporação afirma que o trabalho elaborado pelos delegados não seguiu orientações definidas pelo presidente do STF , ministro Edson Fachin.

Em resposta ao MJ, Andrei afirmou que a equipe encarregada "apresentou relatórios em desacordo com o que fora estipulado", citando apenas três ministros do STF e não "todas as menções encontradas sem exceção", e contendo "elementos que extrapolaram o 'caráter estritamente descritivo'".

"Por fim, reitera-se que não houve qualquer avocação ou interferência em investigação criminal, tratando-se de providência administrativa no interesse do estrito cumprimento de determinação judicial e nos termos da lei".

Os novos relatórios deverão ser individualizados e abordar todos os ministros do STF que tenham sido citados, e não apenas Moraes, Nunes Marques e Toffoli. Segundo o blog do Valdo Cruz no g1, há menções aos ministros André Mendonça, Luiz Fux e Gilmar Mendes.

Diretor-geral da PF, Andrei Passos Rodrigues, é ouvido na CPI do Crime Organizado — Foto: Andressa Anholete/Agência Senado

O chefe da PF também rebateu rumores sobre divisão interna ou perda de autonomia. Ele acrescentou que os mais de 16 mil servidores atuam de forma coesa e republicana.

"A quem interessa enfraquecer a Polícia Federal? Por mais que ataquem a instituição e a mim e a meus familiares diretamente, não irão nos intimidar, porque sabemos o que está por trás de tudo", declarou Rodrigues.

Sem fazer referências diretas, o diretor-geral declarou que "muitos tentam minar" a credibilidade da PF.

"Não há crise, racha interno, muito menos perda de autonomia na Polícia Federal. Somos mais de 16 mil servidores, espalhados em mais de 100 unidades da PF, trabalhando por um bem comum. Não se pode conceber que vozes isoladas queiram se achar maiores que a própria PF. É preciso entender definitivamente que a PF tem um trabalho sério e imparcial", acrescentou.

O diretor também disse que, para ele, a hierarquia e a disciplina são inafastáveis, assim como a autonomia técnica e a responsabilidade funcional.

articles.title: Senado vota pacote do governo de ajuste das contas; falta analisar 4 propostas para alterar o texto principal | G1
articles.standfirst: Uma das propostas é retirar a restrição ao uso de créditos pelas empresas para abater impostos.
articles.summary: Uma das propostas é retirar a restrição ao uso de créditos pelas empresas para abater impostos.
articles.body:
O Senado deve concluir nesta terça-feira (17) a votação do pacote do governo de ajuste das contas. Uma das propostas é retirar do texto a restrição ao uso de créditos pelas empresas para abater imposto.

O texto principal do projeto foi aprovado no plenário do Senado na quinta-feira (12). O governo calcula que as medidas vão ter um impacto de até R$ 60 bilhões no Orçamento de 2027. O projeto cria novos mecanismos para conter as despesas quando houver risco para o cumprimento da meta de resultado das contas públicas. Os gastos não poderão aumentar mais do que 2% acima da inflação. Hoje, podem crescer até 2,5%.

No caso de risco de descumprimento da meta, o governo também fica autorizado a limitar a compensação de créditos tributários pelas empresas. Esses créditos são os valores que uma empresa pode descontar dos tributos a pagar porque, por exemplo, recolheu impostos a mais nas operações anteriores do negócio ou venceu disputas na Justiça. O governo só definirá os percentuais de redução dos créditos após a aprovação do projeto.

O governo trabalha para concluir a votação no Senado nesta terça-feira (17). Falta analisar quatro destaques, propostas para alterar o texto principal. Um deles é o que retira do projeto essa limitação de créditos tributários. Associações de empresas de vários setores têm se manifestado contra essa medida do governo que causa grande impacto nos negócios. Com a limitação na compensação tributária, muitas empresas terão que pagar uma parcela maior de impostos ao não usar todo o crédito a que tem direito e o valor ainda ficaria a critério do governo.

Senado vota pacote do governo de ajuste das contas; falta analisar 4 propostas para alterar o texto principal — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

O senador Alan Rick, do Republicanos, é o autor do destaque. Ele afirma que as empresas foram pegas de surpresa no fim do ano e não tem como abrir mão do dinheiro dos créditos:

"Imagine você que tem uma empresa, tem crédito tributário para ser compensado e você tá contando com isso para poder pagar décimo terceiro salário, férias, pagar os investimentos que fez na empresa e de repente o governo diz: 'Não, eu vou pagar do jeito que eu quiser, quando quiser'. É terrível e nós vamos buscar aprovar nossa emenda supressiva e garantir que haja previsibilidade, segurança jurídica para o setor produtivo brasileiro".

O pesquisador Rafael Barbosa, do FGV IBRE, afirma que a medida aumenta a incerteza para as empresas e não ataca o crescimento dos gastos obrigatórios:

"Essa é uma medida que é inócua do ponto de vista para controlar os gastos públicos ou controlar, estabilizar a dívida. O ponto principal para estabilizar a dívida é a gente atacar de frente o problema dos gastos obrigatórios, ou seja, mesmo que o governo faça isso, dificulte a vida das empresas, consiga arrecadar temporariamente algum recurso, o crescimento dos gastos obrigatórios vai em algum momento forçar o governo a tomar uma outra medida. Ou seja, não é uma medida que a gente acredita que vá funcionar na prática para controlar a dívida pública".

Depois de o Senado concluir a votação, o texto seguirá para análise dos deputados.

articles.title: Indicted Virginia state senator pushes to sanction Blanche, Patel over public comments
articles.summary: Attorneys for Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas (D) are pushing for sanctions against several top Trump administration officials over public comments they made when announcing her indictment on public corruption charges last month. Lucas’s lawyers asked a federal judge on Sunday to issue sanctions against FBI Director Kash Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche and First…
articles.body:
Attorneys for Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas (D) are pushing for sanctions against several top Trump administration officials over public comments they made when announcing her indictment on public corruption charges last month.

Lucas’s lawyers asked a federal judge on Sunday to issue sanctions against FBI Director Kash Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche and First Assistant U.S. Attorney Theophani Stamos for “extrajudicial statements” made during an Oct. 22 press conference “opining on Senator Lucas’s guilt and the merits of the case at the inception and during the pendency of this prosecution.”

“This is the type of conduct for which this Court has imposed criminal-contempt sanctions,” the attorneys wrote to the judge. “The Court should sanction these violations and enter curative relief to protect Senator Lucas’s right to a fair trial by an impartial jury and to deter such conduct in the future.”

There are strict ethical and professional rules surrounding the public comments lawyers and law enforcement personnel can make outside of court, including — but not limited to — prohibiting any statement that concerns “any opinion as to the accused’s guilt or innocence or as to the merits of the case or the evidence in the case.”

The motion was filed a day before Lucas was set to be arraigned in a federal courtroom in Newport News, Va., on five charges connected to her alleged role in a $4.5 million drug trafficking and money laundering scheme tied to a family cannabis business.

Lucas, the president pro tempore of the Virginia Senate, is accused of using her political power as chair of the Virginia Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to influence legislation and obtain licenses that financially benefited her family members and close associates.

Prosecutors alleged in an October indictment that Lucas orchestrated a five-year scheme that involved the distribution of roughly 100 kilograms of marijuana in the eastern Virginia area.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) claimed she and several others, including her daughters and grandson, used various business entities to “disguise the proceeds of illegal marijuana distribution” and Lucas’ position to insulate the illicit enterprise from criminal scrutiny.

“The purpose of her enterprise included trafficking large quantities of illegal marijuana, creating generational wealth for members and associates of her criminal enterprise, recycling drug proceeds to expand the operation that she launched and created, and steering marijuana licenses to entities in which members held financial interest during her time as Virginia state senator,” Patel said during the Oct. 22 press conference, describing the alleged conduct as “truly the epitome of hypocrisy for a public official.”

Lucas’s lawyers claim that Patel sought to “inflate the seriousness of the criminal conduct alleged in the indictment” by exaggerating the quantity of drugs that were sold and the amount of money made, a “clear” violation of court rules.

“The Department remains confident in its case and will not comment further on pending litigation,” a Justice Department spokesperson said on Monday. The Hill has also reached out to the FBI for comment.

Authorities raided Lucas’s office in Portsmouth, Va., in May, as well as two nearby dispensaries that purported to sell legal hemp and CBD products. Federal agents reportedly seized marijuana and firearms from the two shop locations, both of which were tied to what the DOJ called the “Lucas Enterprise.”

It is legal to possess recreational marijuana in Virginia, but the state’s retail cannabis market is not set to open until July 2027, so it is unclear how Lucas would have been able to obtain a license at the time of the alleged offenses.

Lucas’s arrest sent shockwaves through the political world, with some criticizing the Justice Department for bringing charges against an elected official so close to the midterm elections. The investigation predated the second Trump administration, according to DOJ officials.

“This is a long-running case, as alleged in the indictment,” Blanche said during the press conference. “People can criticize all they want, but it was time to bring the charges. The grand jury returned an indictment, and we made the arrests.”

Lucas’s lawyers claim Blanche “was vouching for the political motives” of the investigation when he defended the timing.

“This again is nothing more than gratuitous vouching for the criminal investigation and the guilt of Senator Lucas, something any trial lawyer would be prohibited from doing even at the trial of a criminal defendant,” they wrote in Sunday’s filing.

Lucas has served in the Virginia Senate for more than three decades and isn’t up for reelection until 2027. But she’ll be facing some headwinds when lawmakers return to Richmond in January as some push for an internal investigation.

State Sen. Bryce Reeves (R) has filed a resolution that would direct the Committee on Privileges and Elections to review the allegations in the indictment and calls for Lucas to be expelled from the chamber.

“Based on the very long affidavit that the FBI has, and her failure to list all these other companies on her ethics form, I thought it’d be necessary to step up and try to do something about the corruption,” Reeves told former Rep. Matt Gaetz (R-Fla.) during a recent appearance on One America News Network.

articles.title: California sues OpenAI, alleges it endangered the public by building AI without safeguards
articles.summary: California says the company behind ChatGPT 'misled and endangered the public' by testing AI models without safeguards.
articles.body:
California sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging it failed to rein in powerful, potentially dangerous artificial intelligence technology.

California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta's office said the San Francisco-based company behind ChatGPT "misled and endangered the public by knowingly developing and testing advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models without the safeguards and monitoring necessary to adequately protect the public."

Bonta's office alleged that an AI attack in July — in which OpenAI models broke out of an offline space , connected to the internet and hacked into Hugging Face, a rival AI company — was "entirely foreseeable in light of OpenAI's choice to test models it knew to be dangerous in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight."

OpenAI spokesman Drew Pusateri said in a statement to The Times that the lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab."

He said the company has "undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity" since the Hugging Face incident, including by strengthening safeguards across its systems and creating a "framework for additional identification and disclosure" of unintended activity, and will "continue to engage" with Bonta's office "to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry."

The company previously called the Hugging Face attack a "warning shot" and pledged to make investments to prevent similar incidents.

Bonta's office said the company's "disregard for the public safety" created a "public nuisance" in violation of a law prohibiting businesses from engaging in "unfair" or "fraudulent" practices.

"While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability," Bonta said.

The lawsuit directly challenges a rapidly growing industry that has been a massive economic boon to the state . An August report found that in 2026, California attracted $366 billion in industry-related venture capital — about 90% of all venture capital in the U.S., and three times more than every other state combined.

The funding — half of it linked to just two companies, Anthropic and OpenAI — helped the state move from a multibillion-dollar fiscal deficit to a multibillion-dollar surplus, according to budget projections.

The lawsuit also follows a public reckoning in recent months over claims from industry insiders that AI technology is developing too rapidly and poses an existential threat to human society.

OpenAI has suggested in the past that one of the better ways to ensure AI is safe is to release it broadly. Chief Executive Sam Altman and Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki once wrote on their company's website that its "first commitment is to build AI in service of humanity" and in a way that empowers "people broadly," not just a concentrated few.

"We believe the safer future is one where power is broadly distributed, so more of the world can participate in building a resilience ecosystem," they wrote. They went on to say that "AI resilience refers to the collective organizations, systems, and individuals that society could put in place to anticipate, withstand, adapt to, and rapidly recover from AI-driven disruptions."

They compare building AI safeguards to making automobiles safer by improving road infrastructure and enforcing seat belt and traffic laws. "The goal wasn't to stop people from driving — it was to make a powerful technology resilient enough for widespread use," they wrote.

The company called the Hugging Face attack "evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed."

Bonta announced a formal investigation into the Hugging Face attack and served the company with an investigative subpoena in September — part of a broader probe of mounting cybersecurity incidents involving OpenAI, Bonta's office said. On Monday, his office said such attacks "may just be the tip of the iceberg," but the scope of the problem isn't fully known because OpenAI hasn't answered "detailed questions" about them.

In its own review of the Hugging Face hack alongside third-party auditors, OpenAI found that more than 700 AI agents began coordinating with each other via thousands of messages to escape containment and begin the unsanctioned attack. Subsequent investigations revealed similar testing of unreleased AI models had resulted in other cyberattacks, including on Wikipedia and government websites — sparking fears that future hacks could undermine increasingly critical infrastructure.

Earlier this year, Trump signed a voluntary safety-standards accord with AI executives to establish AI protocols. California has gone further, passing more than two dozen AI-related bills, including measures that establish a state framework for independent AI safety auditors .

Separate from the case in California, OpenAI announced Monday that it will allow four independent third-party evaluators to monitor how its systems behave as they are tested ahead of public release.

"This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated," OpenAI said in a statement.

Bonta said Monday that securing public safety will require litigation and legislation in all 50 states and at the federal and international levels — and that he refused to accept that society should "pass off the blame to machines" while letting those who create them escape accountability.

"The people who created, who create, and operate these machines need to accept the responsibility for their actions," Bonta said at a news conference Monday.

"Whether it's a car or a toy, the law is simple: Don't build or test things that can hurt people without proper safeguards," he said.

Bonta's office said it is encouraging "anyone with information relevant to this case" to contact it at oag.ca.gov/report .

He said his office is also watching other AI companies "closely," but declined to elaborate.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Ground stop chaos spurs fight in Congress over air traffic control funding
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is asking for $50 billion to help modernize air traffic control systems after a widespread failure halted flights.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON – Congress is under pressure to act after air traffic control issues grounded flights nationwide last week , setting up a new funding fight on Capitol Hill and further complicating lawmakers' efforts to avoid another government shutdown before Christmas.

Trump administration officials are pleading for billions of additional dollars to modernize what they acknowledge is an aging system. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said he's asking lawmakers to fast-track a $50 billion package to prevent further communications malfunctions like the one that derailed air travel before the weekend.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are already voicing skepticism about the request, with Democrats pointing to unused Federal Aviation Administration funds and Republicans balking at the topline number.

Despite those concerns, there's a near-universal understanding on Capitol Hill that the FAA's systems are in desperate need of a revamp. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, indicated on CNN over the weekend that while Congress has "given the administration what they asked for," there could be an openness to additional spending.

"If they need more, they should come up and justify it," he said. "I will support what is necessary to have a safe system and a reliable system."

This is what the FAA nationwide ground stop looked like at airports

The new funding request could quickly become another variable in the ongoing negotiations to avoid another shutdown after Dec. 11, when government funding is set to run out. Several Senate Democrats have signaled a willingness in recent weeks to risk a shutdown to pressure President Donald Trump to end the war in Iran .

According to federal officials, the air travel meltdown that disrupted Americans' lives and stranded them at airports was caused by a breakdown in the FAA's communications network. It was prompted by the replacement of a router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas , as part of an ongoing effort to switch out old copper wires with fiber-optic cable. Trump and those around him have since blamed the problem on outdated technology.

"I have systems that are from the '90s. I have radar that are from the '60s and '70s," Duffy said on CNN before emphasizing a need for more funding.

Trump weighed in on the situation for the first time Nov. 16.

"Essentially, what you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack," the president told reporters. He said he was "sure" Congress would soon send more dollars to the FAA.

Duffy is expected to sit in on Senate Republicans' weekly lunch on Nov. 17, where he'll continue to make the case for his funding request.

As of Nov. 16, he had not released comprehensive details on how the $50 billion request would be spent. Before upping his ask, however, Duffy spent the last few months pitching an initial $30 billion.

Sen. John Kennedy, R-Louisiana, who told USA TODAY he'd be supportive of appropriating more money, said he wasn't sure why the request increased "overnight."

"I understand we have inflation, but it's not that dramatic," he said half-jokingly. "They just need to do a better job of explaining it to us."

Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-North Carolina, expressed the same sentiments, saying "people have got to explain to me really even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion."

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he, too, wanted clarification.

"There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," he told reporters. Senate Republicans more broadly have already "attempted to do what we can to ensure that the concerns they have about modernization are being addressed."

Democrats are signaling an early frustration with Duffy's request.

They've spent the last few days pointing to a $12.5 billion allocation in Trump's so-called "One Big, Beautiful Bill" meant specifically for air traffic control system upgrades. According to Washington Rep. Eric Larsen, the top Democrat on the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, $11 billion of that remains unspent.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the powerful House Appropriations Committee, called Duffy's funding ask a "$50 billion ransom without a real plan to deliver."

"Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA's systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner," she said in a statement. "Right now, it is clear that we lack such a partner."

Some Republicans have similar questions.

"They have funds available, near as I can tell, that have not been contracted," said Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, adding he has questions for Duffy about "why they haven't spent the money they've got."

Duffy has defended the Transportation Department, saying all of that tranche of money will be spent and deployed by the end of 2028. None of the money Congress included in that batch of funding, he argued, could go toward fully replacing new telecommunications architecture.

"They were very specific on how we spend the 12.5, and none of the money goes to this telecom that I have to build," Duffy said on ABC News . "They need to give me additional money to finish that project."

Transportation Department and FAA staff will brief congressional staffers about the latest funding request this week.

Zachary Schermele is the congressional correspondent for USA TODAY. Reach him by email at zschermele@usatoday.com and on Signal @zachschermele.02. Follow him on X at @ZachSchermele.

articles.title: Khanna proposes $1,700 Iran war refund checks for Americans
articles.summary: Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) on Monday proposed $1,700 refund checks to reimburse Americans for the economic impact of the Iran war. Khanna, a progressive and potential 2028 presidential contender, said on social media the checks would be sent to every American to cover higher gas, food and electricity prices caused by disruptions to oil transport…
articles.body:
Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) on Monday proposed $1,700 refund checks to reimburse Americans for the economic impact of the Iran war.

Khanna, a progressive and potential 2028 presidential contender, said on social media the checks would be sent to every American to cover higher gas, food and electricity prices caused by disruptions to oil transport routes due to the war. A frequent critic of the war, Khanna said Democrats were given an opportunity through their midterm victories.

“I want to give every American family a $1,700 check to make them whole for the war in Iran,” Khanna said.

The war has cost American households an average of $2,000 since its start, according to Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics. The cost of gas has risen to average highs of more than $4 per gallon, and it sits at $3.81 per gallon as of Monday afternoon. Diesel is about two dollars more expensive per gallon compared with a year ago.

Khanna called on Democrats to vote on his measure almost immediately after taking over the chamber. The party won a larger-than-expected House majority and campaigned on its commitment to address affordability concerns.

“Democrats have a chance to deliver. The first week in January, the House and Senate must pass a refund check to Americans,” Khanna wrote on social media . “Let’s put it on Trump’s desk.”

President Trump has repeatedly said that higher prices are worth it to prevent a nuclear Iran. He said gas prices will fall once the war is over but has continued the conflict and recently said a deal to end the war was not needed .

Khanna has been traveling the country campaigning for midterm candidates as he contemplates a presidential run. As a staunch progressive, he could fill the far-left lane in the Democratic primary field, potentially alongside another popular progressive — Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.).

The California legislator has also called for Congress to eliminate all funding for the Iran war, which would effectively deny any ability for the Trump administration to continue operations. The cost of the war topped $47 billion in October .

“I would stop the funding. The House and the Senate should stop the funding for any further actions in the Iran war. That’s what we did to stop the Vietnam War, and we need to stop this war in Iran,” Khanna said prior to the midterm elections .

articles.title: Joe Rogan slams Trump, says MAGA betrayed ‘podcast bros’
articles.summary: So to Trump and his party, I say this: Take Joe Rogan’s warning seriously, and make the economy work for the people who voted you in to power two years ago.
articles.body:
Joe Rogan is back, with a stinging indictment of President Trump’s approach to the midterms.

The independent commentator slammed the administration for betraying its core commitments to the people who elected Trump in 2024, saying that the war in Iran and aggressive immigration enforcement were big mistakes that cost Republicans the election.

Here was Rogan noting that Trump didn’t just lose the podcast bros — he lost just about everybody.

Rogan correctly identifies that Trump’s successes in the first place were due to catering to the policy agenda of the podcast bros, including Joe Rogan, Theo Von and Andrew Schulz. Trump made promises like “no new wars,” and then he broke them. This clearly hurt Republicans, as the exact demographic they had won just two years ago did not show up for them in 2026.

Now, I’ve noticed many conservatives correctly pointing out that tariffs, the war and overzealous immigration enforcement are what hurt the GOP. The problem is, every conservative I talk to seems to like one of those things and not the other two, and so ends up making excuses. If you like the tariffs, you blame the war and ICE. If you think the war is necessary, you blame tariffs and ICE. If you agree with mass deportations, you blame tariffs and the war.

But really, it was all three of those things, and also affordability, which become a very serious and under-scrutinized issue for young men in particular. The right is quickly losing this demographic again, because of a betrayal of core promises.

Dave Smith, another podcast bro type commentator, brought this up on a recent interview . Take a look.

Of course, I don’t think it’s literally true that you need to be making $1 million to afford a middle-class lifestyle. In my home state of Michigan, for example, the median household income is around $65,000, and that is considered middle class. Michigan has the 28th highest income of the 50 states, so it’s about in the middle of the pack.

A person making $65,000 a year should be able to buy a house that costs between $200,000 and $300,000, and the average price of a house in Michigan does indeed fall within that range. There are plenty of states where housing is even cheaper.

All that said, I understand where Smith is coming from. There are a lot more economic opportunities in cities, and it’s rational for young people to want to move there to chase higher-paying jobs. But housing prices in many cities — New York City, Chicago, Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., where I live — are astronomical.

Moreover, having kids is expensive. Education is expensive. Child care is expensive. These things are highly regulated and subjected to various governmental constraints that drive up the price; D.C., for instance, keeps trying to mandate that day care workers have degrees in early childhood education, which lowers the available supply.

When I hear young men complain that they’re making good money but still aren’t rich enough to start families, I think this is primarily what they have in mind: housing and then education and child care for any kids down the line. Again, there are places where this isn’t so pricey, or if you live near your own family and can get grandparents to babysit. But if you’re on your own, in an expensive city or near one, where the supply of housing is artificially constrained by regulation and day care costs most of your entire salary, I could understand how you might feel like a middle-class lifestyle is perpetually just out of reach.

Keep in mind that all of this is downstream of some of the bad economic policies of this administration and the previous one. Tariffs raise the prices of good and services. Wars destroy economic value. High taxes, regulation and spending hurt your pocketbook. So many politicians seem to forget this.

At the same time, politicians in both parties seem inclined to want to reduce the burden for every group of Americans except young professionals who want to start families. Michigan’s Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed wants to freeze property taxes for retirees but not younger homeowners, even though retirees tend to have much more wealth and also derive most of the government benefits — i.e., Social Security and Medicare.

If I were advising the Republican Party on how to win back young men, I would be laser focused on guaranteeing them a middle-class life. And I would do that but implementing not big government handouts but free market reforms: income and property tax reductions for everyone, not just older Americans, tipped workers or other highly specific groups; licensing, zoning and regulatory reform; school choice, etc.

So to Trump and his party, I say this: Take Joe Rogan’s warning seriously, and make the economy work for the people who voted you in to power two years ago.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.body:
Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) explained a post he made on Election Night in which he exclaimed that “DEI is back,” saying it was meant to be cheeky.

In a video posted to the social platform X early on Nov. 4 , Khanna said, “Tonight, DEI is back as America celebrated diversity and inclusion.”

“Likely three Black governors, the first Latina governor in Texas, the first Muslim American senator, the first gay senator. I love this America,” the Golden State Democrat continued, referencing notable wins in this year’s elections.

In an interview with CNN’s Kasie Hunt on Friday, Khanna was asked about the strategy behind his post.

“I was being tongue in cheek, but here was my point: Why do we have to accept their term — the right wing’s terms of DE and I? What does DE and I mean? Diversity, that’s a good thing.” Khanna said in his CNN appearance.

“Inclusion. You don’t think it’s inclusive that Mississippi elected its first Black senator after the protests of Fannie Lou Hamer, after Medgar Evers, after Emmett Till? Equity. You don’t think that there should be equity for Black and brown voters?” he added. “So, I was just saying, ‘I’m not going to let the right wing define those terms.’”

Diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives are usually aimed at promoting equity and fairness in institutions, especially when it comes to the issues of racism, homophobia and sexism.

Since he returned to the White House last year, President Trump has taken action to get rid of DEI programs within the federal government. articles.title: Judge sets retrial date for Lindsay Clancy
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy appeared Monday in a Massachusetts courtroom, where she learned she will face a retrial in connection with the deaths of her three young children.
articles.body:
DEDHAM, Mass. ( WPRI ) – Lindsay Clancy appeared Monday in a Massachusetts courtroom, where she learned she will face a retrial in connection with the deaths of her three young children.

Judge William Sullivan said the new trial is set for March 29, 2027.

The Plymouth County District Attorney’s Office did not say what charges Clancy would be retried for, but one of the prosecutors said it would require a jury. It’s unclear if prosecutors will try her on the same charges or a reduced charge.

Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington, however, said that Monday’s development “all but confirms they intend to retry first-degree murder.”

Last week, a judge denied Clancy’s motion to have her charges dismissed after her defense claimed the judge shouldn’t have declared a mistrial in September when jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict.

They argued that the judge should have removed the one juror who favored conviction, then allowed the deliberations to continue. But Sullivan disagreed, saying he saw no other option than declaring a mistrial.

Clancy does not deny that she strangled her three young children with exercise bands back in January 2023, but her lawyer has argued that she had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behavior.

Her two oldest children, 5-year-old Cora Clancy and 3-year-old Dawson Clancy, were rushed to the hospital and later pronounced dead. Her youngest child, 7-month-old Callan Clancy, spent several days in the hospital before dying from his injuries .

The 36-year-old attempted to take her own life after the murders by jumping out of a second-story window. She survived the fall but suffered a severe spinal cord injury and is now paralyzed from the waist down.

articles.title: Dana White after press secretary stunt: ‘I want nothing to do with politics’
articles.summary: UFC President and CEO Dana White on Saturday said he wants “nothing to do with politics” following the stunt last week where he seemed poised to become the next White House press secretary. President Trump wrote on Truth Social earlier this month that he had offered the job to White, who share a friendship. The…
articles.body:
UFC President and CEO Dana White on Saturday said he wants “nothing to do with politics” following the stunt last week where he seemed poised to become the next White House press secretary.

President Trump wrote on Truth Social earlier this month that he had offered the job to White, who share a friendship. The pair took questions at an impromptu press conference last Monday. Trump had said the day before that he was joking.

“You’ll never see me involved in politics. I want nothing to do with politics,” White told President Trump’s daughter-in-law Lara Trump on Fox News’s “ My View with Lara Trump .”

“But, as far as this business goes, I’m in boxing now,” he continued. “This is my first year involved in boxing. So I’m just always focused on what’s next with my business and where we want to take it, places we’ve never been before.”

Lara Trump asked about how he “almost inadvertently becoming the next press secretary,” prompting White to reply that it was an “amazing experience.”

“Literally when I was pulling in the gates of the White House, his assistant called and said, ‘Hey, we’re going to take you right down to the press room, he wants you,'” White said. “I was like, ‘What? This is crazy.’ It was a very unique and crazy 48 hours for me.”

He said he was at a fight in London when President Trump called him and told him he put the Truth Social post out. White told reporters at the press briefing that his life had “been insane” the last 24 hours, receiving calls from “every media outlet.”

By the end of the briefing, he reiterated that he did not accept the president’s offer, prompting President Trump to quip, “I am devastated to hear this.”

The UFC head told Lara Trump that he wants to remain in his current role, saying that his “ceiling is 8 billion” people in the world, with the hope of them tuning in to company.

White also recalled when the president floated the idea of hosting a UFC fight at the White House. It was on a Saturday, and by Monday, “he already had people calling talking about doing it.” The executive mansion hosted the UFC Freedom 250 fight in June as part of celebrations for the nation’s 250th birthday and the president’s 80th birthday.

“So, yeah, when he says he’s going to do something, he does it,” White said.

The White House has not had a press secretary since political commentator Katie Zacharia held the post for less than a week . She left the administration after reports emerged that she had marketed herself as an attorney without ever passing the bar exam. Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt departed in August .

Leavitt’s departure into Zacharia’s brief tenure marked the longest vacancy in the role’s near 100-year-long history at 46 days.

articles.title: Nationwide ground stop could cost US airlines hundreds of millions
articles.summary: Airline executives support modernising FAA systems as US Transportation Secretary Duffy seeks $50bn from Congress.
articles.body:
Following the nationwide ground stop last week , United States airlines could face a financial hit of hundreds of millions of dollars even as airline executives press for increased investment in ageing air traffic control infrastructure .

The four largest US airlines – American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines – could face a combined hit of $345m to pretax earnings, according to brokerage firm Bernstein.

The effects of Friday’s ground stop continued to ripple through airline schedules on Monday, with more than 18,500 flights within, into or out of the US cancelled since the disruption began, according to FlightAware data.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC on Monday that the wider impact of the disruption could run into the “billions of dollars”. No official estimate of the total economic cost has been released yet.

Flights were grounded across the country for more than four hours on Friday, and the disruption continued to affect airline schedules over the weekend.

Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian also said the financial impact could run into the “billions”, telling Fortune on Monday that the disruption underscored the need for greater investment in the country’s air traffic control infrastructure.

Bastian pointed to the vast sums investors are putting into artificial intelligence and data centres, adding that the US should also be investing in its aviation system.

“We can’t even get $50bn to fix our skies,” he said.

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby agreed that the disruption should be a “call to action”, saying the air traffic control system needed greater investment in modern technology to improve its reliability.

Transportation Secretary Duffy has asked US Congress for $50bn for air traffic control and airport infrastructure upgrades, an addition to the $12.5bn lawmakers approved for air traffic control modernisation last year.

The existing system relies on outdated equipment and needs a comprehensive overhaul, he said.

But Democrats have questioned the request, saying only about $1bn of the $12.5bn already approved has been spent so far.

On Sunday, US President Donald Trump called on Congress to approve the funding, arguing that the upgrades should be carried out all at once rather than in stages.

“We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The funding debate is moving into a narrow window for congressional action. The House and Senate are scheduled to convene once more before the end of the year.

Speaker Mike Johnson has said lawmakers will take up the administration’s funding request during the current Congress’s lame-duck session, but Democrats have demanded more information on how the money will be spent.

The precise cause of Friday’s failure remains under investigation. Duffy has said the problem began at a remote Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) site in Arkansas where workers from defence contractor L3Harris were replacing ageing copper wiring with fibre-optic cables.

The Government Accountability Office, the congressional watchdog, raised concerns about the FAA’s management of its modernisation programme in a September report. It found that the agency had not developed an integrated schedule for the first phase of upgrades, and warned that poor planning increased the risk of disrupting air traffic control operations.

articles.title: 'Everybody's shell-shocked': GOP operatives face 2028 prospects after midterm defeats
articles.summary: Some argued JD Vance may no longer be the presumptive 2028 nominee.
articles.body:
On Election Day, many Republicans were bracing for a tough outcome, but not what has been described as a blue tsunami.

"I thought that we were going to keep the Senate," former Republican National Committee Chair Ronna McDaniel told ABC News. "I didn't think that Democrats could make inroads in states like South Carolina and Kansas and even Texas."

Democrats did more than make inroads. They flipped eight GOP-held Senate seats and as of Monday, Democrats hold 256 House seats to the GOP's 170. There are still some outstanding races as of Monday: nine House races and one Senate race.

Over a dozen Republican donors and operatives told ABC News that the Republican Party is still in shock after the sweeping midterm losses. They pointed to a message that focused on culture wars and failed to reach voters squeezed by costs tied to the war in Iran and a Latino coalition that slipped away. Some argued Vice President JD Vance may no longer be the presumptive 2028 nominee. Vance, who has not formally announced he is launching a presidential bid for 2028, has acknowledged "there's a chance" he won't run in 2028.

The president's record- low approval ratings were also difficult to ignore, some said.

"The losses are all about Trump," said one Republican consultant who worked on races out West and spoke to ABC News on the condition of anonymity. "This was a total rebuke of Donald Trump, both him personally and his politics."

RNC National Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement that Republicans will "continue to put America first," highlighting that the RNC raised $130 million, sending more than $60 million directly to Republican campaigns.

When reached for comment, the White House emphasized Trump's signature tax legislation and said that Trump will continue to work for the American people.

"Under President Trump's leadership, this administration has signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, secured the border, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, and locked in nearly 20 trade deals. President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told ABC News in a statement.

Vance's office, when asked for comment, deferred to the White House.

The donors and operatives who spoke to ABC News agreed Republicans lacked a clear message on affordability -- a key issue for voters.

"We need to talk about pocketbook issues. We didn't do that," said Sarah Chamberlain, president and CEO of the Republican Main Street Partnership, a group that fundraises for moderate Republicans.

T.W. Arrighi, a Republican strategist who worked on Republican Darline Graham's Senate race, said Democrats were talking about affordability "in a more tangible way than we were … We have conservative solutions to these issues, we just didn't deliver."

A GOP strategist involved in many 2026 races said the party's turnout operation will likely take much of the blame. ABC News' analysis of early voting in Texas and Georgia a week before Election Day showed greater Democratic enthusiasm.

"We just weren't hitting the numbers we needed to hit of just sheer Republicans voting. A lot of them stayed home, and we knew that was happening," the strategist said.

The Republican consultant who worked on races out West added that Republicans had "no choice" but to run on culture war issues because of the high costs brought on by the Iran war.

"You can't tell people to ignore your lying eyes," the source said. "[Republicans] had no choice but to go down the culture-war road because we couldn't talk about the economy."

Trump said in a phone interview with Fox News on election night that he was "a little bit surprised" by the midterm results and added that part of the reason was the Iran war, directly linking it to gas prices.

In a social media post after the election, Trump wrote that Republicans would have been more successful had he been on the ballot.

According to the ABC News Voter Poll, in 2026, Latino voters nationally supported Democratic House candidates by a 30-point margin. In 2024, it was a 13-point margin.

Trump acknowledged his mass-deportation policies may have been "too tough" in an interview with CBS News' "60 Minutes" after the midterms.

Mike Madrid, a GOP consultant who studies Latino voting behavior, said "there is no question that the ICE stuff and deportations played a role."

"There's also no question that the economy was the No. 1 factor. But in some districts, like south Texas, they're one and the same. Immigration is the economy there," Madrid said.

Democrats swept every congressional district along the southern border, flipping several Republican-held seats in Texas.

Billionaire donor John Catsimatidis told ABC News that the losses came down to the war in Iran and "ICE being too tough on waiters and busboys."

Immigration enforcement under the Trump administration has reached local businesses and restaurants. ABC News reported last May that in D.C., federal law enforcement officials visited dozens of restaurants, carry-out spots and bars across several neighborhoods.

RNC Co-Chair KC Crosbie announced on Nov. 5 that she's challenging RNC Chair Joe Gruters, saying the party should "be willing to confront where we fell short."

A source close to Gruters confirmed to ABC News that he is running for reelection.

While Trump has since reaffirmed his support for Gruters, some Republicans questioned Gruters' competence.

"Joe Gruters failed the Republican Party, and I find it puzzling that he believes he deserves to be reelected," said an RNC member.

Florida GOP Chairman Evan Power said in a statement, however, that "Gruters was a key partner in our fight to keep the Free State of Florida red, and he's the leader I trust to keep our party on offense and ready to win in 2028."

McDaniel said "the committee should support whoever the president wants to be the RNC chair."

She added that donors who may be discouraged from giving in the future need an autopsy from the party over what went wrong.

"People are still wondering what happened, and the sooner that a plan is put forward, and they get in the field and they get data … That's going to be what's going to bring donors back. But right now, I think everybody's shell-shocked."

While Vance hasn't ruled out a run in 2028, some donors told ABC News that his proximity to Trump may be a liability.

But a Vance ally who spoke to ABC News cautioned against writing off Vance, comparing it to the 2016 and 2024 election cycles, when different parts of the Republican Party wrote Trump off.

And although Vance is still undecided about a 2028 presidential run, many of Vance's allies expect that he will run for president in 2028, sources confirmed to ABC News Chief Washington Correspondent Jonathan Karl.

Vance's allies say he will decide whether to pursue a White House bid on his own timeline.

But some Republicans see an opening for Secretary of State Marco Rubio to run for president in 2028 following the midterm elections.

Rubio has said he has no plans to run for president in 2028, adding that he would support Vance if he mounted a presidential run.

Catsimatidis said his family has been supporters of Vance, but he has known Rubio for 15 years and considers the nomination "still open."

A Texas-based GOP donor said the next nominee must appeal to "most all Republicans, a majority of independents and a reasonable group of conservative Democrats."

"We're in like stage two with a five-stage model of grief or something. We're not at the writing-checks-for-new-people yet stage," said one donor. "America doesn't want more MAGA."

Scott DesJarlais (R-Tenn.) conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick on Monday in an unexpectedly close race. “I have personally reached out to Ms. Broderick to offer my congratulations and my support on this new undertaking,” the House Republican wrote on Facebook. “I am proud of the standard our office has set in terms of representing…
articles.body:
Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-Tenn.) conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick on Monday in an unexpectedly close race.

“I have personally reached out to Ms. Broderick to offer my congratulations and my support on this new undertaking,” the House Republican wrote on Facebook. “I am proud of the standard our office has set in terms of representing the values, interests, and needs of our district.”

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) has yet to project a winner in the race for Tennessee’s 4th District. Broderick leads the incumbent by about a tenth of a percentage point as of Monday afternoon — 48.87 to 48.73 percent. DDHQ reported Broderick was up on DesJarlais by just over 200 votes.

However, despite being majorly outspent by DesJarlais in a district President Trump carried by 24 points in 2024, Broderick managed to pull out the win.

Broderick said her motivation for getting involved in politics was the Supreme Court overturning Roe v. Wade in 2022. She campaigned on keeping rural hospitals open, protecting responsible gun owners while reducing gun violence, increased oversight on war and defense spending and affordable pre-K education.

She also notably promised to work to decriminalize marijuana and increase oversight on AI companies and data center infrastructure projects, per the Nashville Post .

During his eight terms in the House, DesJarlais supported much of Trump’s agenda including introducing a bill that would have forbidden the Department of Education and other federal departments from cancelling or forgiving student loans.

“We all leave here with our heads held high, and we hope the Fourth District continues to receive the attention and care it so richly deserves,” he wrote Monday. “All of us hope that the new Member of Congress feels the same level of awe and gratitude for this tremendous undertaking that I felt every day I had the privilege of serving.”

articles.title: Clarence Thomas calls foul on California ruling he says could turn citizens into government mouthpieces
articles.summary: Clarence Thomas warns the Supreme Court's refusal to hear a California implicit bias case leaves states free to compel speech from private citizens.
articles.body:
Justice Clarence Thomas warned Monday that the Supreme Court is leaving the door open for states to compel speech from private citizens by not taking up a challenge to a California law.

On Monday, the Supreme Court declined a petition to hear a case from a California physician who argued that the state government was forcing her to make statements she disagreed with while teaching a mandatory course for doctors. Thomas was joined by Justice Samuel Alito in dissenting from the decision, arguing that allowing the law to stand could have implications reaching far beyond the medical field.

The case stems from California's requirement that all its licensed physicians complete 50 hours of state-approved continuing education courses every two years. California requires continuing medical education courses to include instruction on implicit bias, either through examples of how it affects physicians' treatment decisions and health outcomes or strategies for addressing how those biases may contribute to healthcare disparities.

"When, as here, the government does not issue its own messages but instead requires private speakers to communicate the government's viewpoint, the First Amendment applies," Thomas wrote. "A State cannot regulate its way out of First Amendment scrutiny. We should not permit the government-speech doctrine to be wielded as 'a cover for censorship' or a cloak for compelled speech."

Dr. Azadeh Khatibi, who teaches a continuing education course in California, sued the state alongside the right-of-center nonprofit Do No Harm , arguing, as Thomas did, that it compels private instructors to convey a government-favored message in violation of the First Amendment.

"She does not want to include discussion of implicit bias in her courses. It is not relevant to her topics, and it would eat away at the limited time she could use to discuss topics that are relevant," her legal team wrote. "Dr. Khatibi also disagrees that implicit bias is the primary factor driving disparities in healthcare."

California countered that while instructors must include discussion of implicit bias in their courses, they are not required to personally endorse the theory and may openly disagree with it.

"Under the second option, instructors who do not believe that implicit bias exists are free to say so," California wrote in the brief defending its law. "Petitioners are also free to inform CME attendees that any discussion of implicit bias is included solely to comply with state requirements."

California further argued that states must be given broad authority to determine what doctors must do to retain their licenses.

The Ninth Circuit ruled last year that continuing medical education courses constitute government speech because of California's extensive regulation of the medical profession, meaning the state's requirements are not subject to First Amendment free-speech scrutiny.

Thomas, however, disputed California's characterization of whether it was compelling instructors to take certain positions.

"California's implicit-bias-training requirement leaves petitioners no choice but to discuss the topic in a way that affirms the State's view that implicit bias causes 'disparities in health outcomes,'" he wrote.

The justice went on to argue that allowing California's law to go unchallenged could have implications for Americans working in many fields beyond medicine.

"What of other professions whose members California licenses and regulates? At the next statewide legal conference at which lectures are offered for continuing legal education, could California require a keynote speaker to oppose racial preferences in law firm hiring?" Thomas wrote. "Applying the Ninth Circuit's logic, enough government regulation of the field would convert the private speaker's message in each of these hypotheticals into government speech unprotected by the First Amendment. That result does not follow from this Court's precedents, and it certainly does not follow from the Constitution."

Justice Neil Gorsuch also dissented from the court's decision not to hear the case, though he did not sign on to Alito and Thomas' argument. His rationale for wanting to grant certiorari is not publicly known.

The Supreme Court's decision leaves the Ninth Circuit's ruling intact but does not settle whether California's requirement violates the First Amendment.

"Medical professionals should not be compelled by the government to participate in evidence-free implicit bias trainings. It is disappointing the Supreme Court declined to take up our case, but we remain encouraged that some Justices acknowledged the importance of the First Amendment issues at stake in our case, issues that will undoubtedly continue to surface in courts across the country. We will keep fighting for constitutionally-protected free speech to ensure that healthcare providers are never conscripted to deliver the government's message," a spokesperson for Do No Harm told Fox News Digital after publication.
