articles.title: Pete Buttigieg fires back at Trump blaming him for FAA ground stop
articles.summary: Pete Buttigieg, the former Biden administration Transportation Secretary and a potential 2028 presidential candidate, responded Monday to President Donald Tr...
articles.body:
Pete Buttigieg, the former Biden administration Transportation Secretary and a potential 2028 presidential candidate, rejected President Donald Trump's claim on Monday that he was to blame for Friday's historic airspace meltdown.

"As secretary, I made sure to leave air travel in better condition than when we arrived," Buttigieg posted on social media, touting efforts to increase air traffic control staffing and improve safety.

He was responding to a clip of Trump taking questions Monday about the historic ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights nationwide, which federal officials believe may have been spurred by a routine upgrade that went wrong and quickly metastasized into a broad-based communications failure.

In the clip, Trump says that "Buttigieg ruined the system" while accusing Democrats in Congress of withholding necessary funding and setting back the upgrades, despite Republican control of Congress.

Buttigieg, however, rejected the criticism. "I launched a project to transition the FAA's communications system from copper wire to a modern network," he wrote. "I am glad the Trump administration has continued that work, but they have so far failed to explain why their execution of it triggered the worst FAA communications breakdown this century."

Buttigieg was in Denver as the ground stop took effect, appearing at a post-midterms conference featuring several potential 2028 contenders. He kicked off his remarks that night with: "I will be available in the hotel bar following the concert for anybody that needs to rebook their flights."

He is likely to lean on his record leading the Department of Transportation if he runs for president – and face criticism from rivals over it. Ari Emanuel, the brother of Rahm Emanuel, another potential 2028 contender, ripped into Buttigieg on X Friday , saying in part: "You left a failing system in place. THANKS!"

Buttigieg on Monday called for accountability, describing the crisis as "another blow to the public's confidence that the administration can deliver."

"The Trump administration owes Americans an honest accounting of how they have spent the billions of dollars already authorized, clearer answers on why their repair work brought down the entire system on Friday, and an explanation of what they are doing to make sure this failure is not repeated," he wrote.

The White House's rapid response account fired back at Buttigieg, saying: "Actually, your humiliating tenure was one of the biggest displays of incompetence and failure in history."

Facing questions Monday , Trump bristled at scrutiny over his absence from the initial response to a historic airspace meltdown, insisting that he was fully involved in managing the crisis even as he rejected any responsibility for the fallout.

Meanwhile, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy had earlier indicated plans to ask Congress for roughly $50 billion in additional funding for the upgrade work. Trump officials are expected to brief lawmakers on the ground stop and subsequent funding request this week.

Those plans are already facing pushback from Democrats, who have questioned how the administration is allocating an existing $12.5 billion for the FAA that was included in the GOP's partisan centerpiece tax-and-spending legislation last year.

"I've already informed Congress," Trump said of the funding request. "I think the one good thing that comes out of it, I'm sure Congress now will give us the money to fix."

CNN's Adam Cancryn contributed to this report.

articles.title: Outside group files complaint against U.S. attorney for threats against Warren, Blumenthal
articles.summary: Campaign for Accountability, a left-leaning watchdog group, filed a complaint with the Texas Bar against U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz over his threats against Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.). The complaint alleges that some of Reitz’s remarks concerning the senators violated three rules outlined in the Texas…
articles.body:
Campaign for Accountability, a left-leaning watchdog group, filed a complaint with the Texas Bar against U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz over his threats against Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.).

The complaint alleges that some of Reitz’s remarks concerning the senators violated three rules outlined in the Texas Bar Association’s prosecutorial conduct , including barring prosecutors from threatening to pursue charges against someone the attorney “knows is not supported by probable cause.”

“Aaron Reitz is using the power of a federal prosecutor’s office to try to intimidate senators out of doing the jobs for which their constituents elected them. Oversight is not a crime, and Mr. Reitz knows it,” Campaign for Accountability director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a statement.

Reitz previously sent a letter to Warren regarding past comments that she made on CBS News on Nov. 8 . The Massachusetts senator stated that those who made “profits by cheating American families and scamming your investors” should be ready for serious investigations.

He accused her of preparing to target those associated with President Trump Trump when she takes over as chair of the Senate Banking Committee in January.

The attorney, who previously served as Sen. Ted Cruz’s (R-Texas) chief of staff, gave Warren until Nov. 23 to confirm she received the letter and requested she preserve certain records.

Reitz issued similar warnings to Blumenthal, writing in a letter to the senator that his probe into Trump’s White House ballroom threatened the constitutional rights of Americans who contributed to the roughly $400 million project.

He accused Blumenthal of wielding Congress and his role on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations as a “weapon” against Americans for their political associations. Reitz added in a social media post that his investigations were “taking the first step to stop this abuse of power.”

In both letters to Warren and Blumenthal , he warned that failing to preserve relevant documents could carry “significant legal consequences.”

The pair of senators were not formally charged with crimes by Reitz.

In a statement to The Hill, Reitz called the Campaign for Accountability’s complaint “harassing.”

“I will continue my preliminary inquiry unfazed to determine whether certain members of Congress have unlawfully stepped outside the legitimate legislative purpose of their planned committee activities,” he continued.

articles.title: An early look at the 2028 Senate map: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur dives into the next battle for the Senate.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur dives into the next battle for the Senate. Plus, Megan Brand explores how Black voters fueled the inroads Democrats made this year in the South. — Adam Wollner An early look at the 2028 Senate map Analysis by Sahil Kapur In one election night, Democrats turned a deep structural disadvantage in the Senate into an upper hand heading into the next presidential cycle. After Republicans entered the year as favorites to maintain control, Democrats are now on pace to gain nine seats, with NBC News Decision Desk characterizing the Alaska Senate race as a likely victory for former Rep. Mary Pelotla. That would give the party a 56-44 majority, which would be the largest since 2009. It also means the GOP would need to pick up at least six seats to flip control of the chamber in 2028 (and seven if they don’t control the vice presidency). Here’s an early look at the 2028 Senate map. Core battleground: There are six states that were decided by single digits in the last three presidential elections. That includes four Democratic-held seats in Arizona (Mark Kelly), Nevada (Catherine Cortez Masto), Georgia (Raphael Warnock) and Pennsylvania (John Fetterman). Republicans will need to capture all four of those seats to give themselves a realistic shot at the majority in 2028. Of the four Democrats, Fetterman faces the greatest danger of getting a primary challenger after his popularity with Democrats has plummeted. Kelly and Warnock are in the early 2028 presidential conversation; they’ll both have an important decision to make about whether to seek re-election or make a run for the White House. There are also two Republican-held seats in this category: Wisconsin (Ron Johnson) and North Carolina (Ted Budd). Johnson survived in 2022 by just 1 point while Budd won by 3 points in a midterm year in which Democrats were on the receiving end of backlash from voters with Joe Biden in the White House. Extended battleground, red-state edition: There are six states President Donald Trump carried by double digits two years ago that became highly competitive in 2026. The first is Ohio, which Trump won by 11 points in 2024 and Democrat Sherrod Brown won by 5 points this year. Brown’s victory was a special election, so the seat is up again in 2028. It will mark the only double-digit Trump state represented by a Democrat in the next cycle. The others include four Republican-held states where the other Senate seat flipped from red to blue this year: Iowa (Chuck Grassley), Kansas (Jerry Moran), South Carolina (Tim Scott) and, assuming Democrats officially prevail, Alaska (Lisa Murkowski). Rounding out the list is Florida, where GOP Sen. Ashley Moody defeated underfunded progressive Democrat Angie Nixon by less than 3 points. Like Ohio, this was a special election, so Moody will have to run again in two years. Can lightning strike twice? Democrats needed a dream environment (and, in some cases, weak GOP candidates) to make those states competitive in 2026. It’s far from clear they can replicate that in two years. But if they can, a filibuster-proof majority of 60 seats could be within reach for Democrats. Extended battleground, blue-state edition: If Republicans sweep every red and purple state mentioned above, they’ll have picked up five Democratic-held seats, needing at least one more to capture Senate control. That’s where blue-leaning territory comes into focus. Judging by recent presidential elections, New Hampshire (Maggie Hassan) is probably the GOP’s best chance. From there the hill gets much steeper, with seats up in the solidly Democratic states of California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Maryland, New York, Oregon, Vermont and Washington. How difficult are those states? In 2022, Republicans zeroed in on Colorado and Washington as sleeper races after recruiting who they viewed as strong candidates. They ultimately lost both by double digits. It’s almost a mirror image of the rough environment Democrats faced entering 2026 — they needed to win at least two solidly red states to have a shot at Senate control. Now it’s Republicans who would need to win at least one blue state to give themselves a chance. How the tables have turned. How a surge in Black turnout propelled Democrats in key Southern states By Megan Brand Black voters turned out in South Carolina at a level more similar to a presidential election year than a midterm year, according to state data, helping propel Sen.-elect Annie Andrews across the finish line in the longtime red state, while similar patterns powered other Democrats across the country. Political experts and activists say higher Black voter turnout paved the way for Democrats to flip both the House and the Senate, with Democrats making gains in other traditionally red states with large Black populations, including Mississippi. Black voters played key roles in races in Georgia and Louisiana, too. Running underneath it all, the activists told NBC News, was an undercurrent of anger and motivation stemming from redistricting efforts and the Supreme Court’s Louisiana v. Callais decision, which weakened the Voting Rights Act. The April decision kicked off redistricting efforts in some Republican-led states to cut Democratic seats where many Black voters live. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Ex-staffers claim lack of enforcement, "chaos" under Lutnick
articles.summary: Some former Commerce Department officials are describing Howard Lutnick's tenure as secretary as being marked by "chaos," "micromanaging," and what they alle...
articles.body:
Some former Commerce Department officials are describing Howard Lutnick's tenure as secretary as being marked by "chaos," "micromanaging," and what they allege are failures to act on evidence of highly sensitive computer chip smuggling.

A key national security responsibility of the department is investigating and enforcing bans on the export to China and other U.S. adversaries of advanced computer chips used in artificial intelligence and sophisticated weapons.

"There was an inexplicable refusal to use the tools at their disposal for national security over the last year," one former Commerce official told CBS News.

Scrutiny of Lutnick's tenure has heightened in recent days with Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO after admitting an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies believed to be a Chinese spy. China has denied the accusation of spying, calling it "an attempt to smear China."

As the scandal has unfolded, senior officials and members of Congress have questioned how Nvidia was permitted to sell chips to companies with deep ties to China, and whether the Commerce Department policed those exports effectively.

The answer, according to some of Lutnick's former staff, was not at all.

Four ex-Commerce officials spoke with CBS News, asking to remain anonymous, fearing professional reprisals for discussing their recent experience in government.

"We weren't able to add entities to the Entity List. That was just a complete stop," one former Commerce employee said, referring to the federal list of firms that the U.S. government has banned from buying the most advanced chips due to the belief they would route them to China or other adversaries.

Another former Commerce official said a whole year passed with no companies added to the list, noting that this was the first time that had happened in 18 years. The Federal Register shows the last time entities were added was Oct. 9, 2025, and the last yearlong gap in additions was in 2008.

The first former staffer said the agency's own enforcement officers found suspicious activity at Southeast Asian sites where Nvidia chips had been delivered, but that Commerce directors allegedly took no action.

Placement on the list triggers more stringent license requirements and creates a higher threshold to prevent sensitive products from getting where they shouldn't, the ex-official said.

Instead, "nothing happened," the ex-official said.

The Biden administration issued AI chip export controls in 2022 and 2023, and in January 2025 issued an interim final rule to block China and other adversaries from obtaining the most advanced AI chips, both directly and through third-party countries.

In May 2025, President Trump's Commerce Department rolled back the rule, arguing it "would have stifled American innovation." Instead, the department said it would strengthen export controls for AI chips by issuing guidance to the industry and public.

There are growing signs that bans on exporting advanced U.S. computer chips have been circumvented in large quantities, according to published reports.

An April 2026 study by AI research nonprofit Epoch estimated between 290,000 and 1.6 million cutting-edge AI chips were smuggled into China in 2024 and 2025, comprising "roughly a quarter of the comput[ing power] China acquired through legal channels or domestic production."

Tech news site The Information reported that at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips allegedly ended up with Chinese companies since 2023 just through companies linked to Alice Huang , the suspected Chinese agent accused of an affair with Nvidia's ousted CEO. The report cited sources close to her for the estimate.

And a former researcher at OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, published a paper last week claiming to have found digital forensic evidence that top Chinese AI models were trained using Nvidia chips banned in China.

One former Commerce staffer described the department under Lutnick as "very chaotic, very frantic," with staff sometimes learning of major policy changes via media reports, including a pivot to allow the sale of Nvidia's H20 and H200 chips to China — the company's second-most advanced tier of GPUs.

"We found out about that in The New York Times," the ex-Commerce official said. "It was pretty clear that the decision was made between Trump and Jensen Huang."

The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment. CBS News has also reached out to the White House for comment.

On Monday the department imposed a new rule requiring licenses for exporting, re-exporting or transferring advanced semiconductors to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore or Thailand, aimed at closing a loophole through which chips were exported to China via an intermediary. But the Commerce Department suggested that its own involvement was limited, describing the rule as "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council—to address remote access to advanced super intelligence (SI) chips and servers."

The department lost two of its most senior and experienced experts shortly after Lutnick took office.

One was Matthew Borman, who served as principal deputy assistant secretary for export administration. Borman had been with the department for over 30 years.

Another veteran official, Eileen Albanese, was let go from her longtime role as director of the Office of National Security Controls. Reuters first reported their departures in February 2025, the same month Lutnick started running the department.

"They kicked off the administration by essentially firing the two most respected people," said one former employee.

A profile on the website of law firm Akin Gump, where Albanese now works, says she played a "key role in the development of U.S. export control policy and regulations for advanced artificial intelligence chips and semiconductor manufacturing tools."

"Matt and Eileen were treasures of the U.S. government," one former Commerce staffer said.

Albanese did not respond to a request for comment. Borman declined to comment.

Former officials said subsequent changes under Lutnick helped prompt an "exodus" of up to 50 skilled staff members over the past 18 months.

Over time, those who departed were among the most experienced officials who dealt with key areas including chips and export control enforcement, the ex-staffers said.

"It was an exodus of the finest engineers and scientists, the key experts on AI, on Russia, on diversion, our key expert on chips. Decades of institutional memory and skill went out," an ex-employee said.

Key roles remain vacant in Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, the department in charge of export controls, according to a registry of current senior federal employees. The principal deputy assistant secretary for export administration, the same role for export enforcement and the chief of staff roles are all currently unfilled, the records say.

Some staff described a bottleneck at the Bureau of Industry and Security, accusing its chief — Jeffrey Kessler, a top deputy to Lutnick — of "micromanaging" and blocking enforcement against companies suspected of smuggling chips.

"He made everything go through him. Literally every possible decision, the most minor things. It's impossible for one person to manage that level of things," one former employee under Lutnick told CBS News.

"He didn't want to make any decisions on his own. He would want you to make a memo and he would say, 'Package it up with options for me to bring to a decision maker,' which always cracked me up. Because it's like, who are you? A concerned citizen?"

"The career workforce felt frustrated and stymied," said one former staffer from the previous administration, who is close to many who remained in the department. "They felt like they were unable to do their jobs because [Kessler and Lutnick] were standing in their way."

The former staff members told CBS News that the critical view of Lutnick and his deputy was widely shared in the department.

Cabinet members have even voiced criticism, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessen t telling CNBC last week that Lutnick failed to follow through on chip ban enforcement supported by Treasury, the State Department and others in the administration.

"Commerce has the pen. You would have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told the channel.

"I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above" a certain sophistication, Bessent said.

articles.title: The Memo: Sean Duffy’s $50B FAA request gets cool reception from Congress
articles.summary: The reverberations from Friday’s massive air traffic ground stop are now being felt on Capitol Hill as the Trump administration pushes for an extra $50 billion in funding for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The push is being spearheaded by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who has been the administration’s principal voice following Friday’s shutdown, which…
articles.body:
The reverberations from Friday’s massive air traffic ground stop are now being felt on Capitol Hill as the Trump administration pushes for an extra $50 billion in funding for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

The push is being spearheaded by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who has been the administration’s principal voice following Friday’s shutdown, which grounded thousands of planes, inconvenienced millions of people and was the longest such ground stop since the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001.

Duffy made a number of media appearances on Sunday, most of which built on the message he had delivered during a hastily convened press conference alongside Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin at the White House on Friday evening.

“I’ve asked, the president’s asked, for $30 billion. I want $50 billion,” Duffy said. “What’s more important than having an air traffic control system that actually works?”

There is general agreement on the pressing need to reinvigorate the nation’s creaking air traffic control (ATC) system. That consensus existed before Friday’s meltdown, but the nationwide ground stop has put a much sharper point on it.

That said, Democrats have expressed considerable skepticism about Duffy’s $50 billion request — and not only because it comes from an administration they largely detest.

In specific terms, the opposition party notes that President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, passed last year, provided $12.5 billion specifically to overhaul the ATC system. This pot of money is not expected to be emptied until 2028.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) complained during a floor speech Monday about the Trump administration having existing funds and then asking for more when “they don’t use” the existing tranche.

Pete Buttigieg, who served as Transportation secretary during the Biden administration and has been a frequent target of conservative criticism, defended his record in a social media post on Monday.

Buttigieg, a possible 2028 presidential contender for the Democrats, wrote, “I support more funding for FAA upgrades, but this episode is another blow to the public’s confidence that the administration can deliver.”

The former Transportation secretary added that the current administration “owes Americans an honest accounting of how they have spent the billions of dollars already authorized, clearer answers on why their repair work brought down the entire system on Friday, and an explanation of what they are doing to make sure this failure is not repeated.”

It was also notable that Buttigieg framed his comments as a response to a clip of Trump where the president charged that “Buttigieg ruined the system.” The president contended that he and the GOP had “been trying to get the money for two years to fix it.”

Elsewhere in those remarks, delivered to reporters on the South Lawn of the White House before setting off on an Asia trip, Trump asserted in relation to Friday’s events: “I don’t take any responsibility. … The only responsibility should be, for 40 years they should have done this.”

There is, in fact, widespread agreement that efforts to upgrade the nation’s ATC system have been seriously lacking.

The most famous, or infamous, example is the Next Generation Air Transportation System that was launched more than 20 years ago, during former President George W. Bush’s time in the White House.

A report last year from the Department of Transportation’s inspector general found that $15 billion of a projected $36 billion had been spent by the end of 2024, but a mere 16 percent of the projected benefits had been achieved by that point.

As the public grappled with the massive disruptions caused last Friday, alarm and exasperation were elevated by the reminder that the ATC system runs on deeply anachronistic systems.

The use of floppy disks is only now being phased out and some part of Friday’s debacle appears to center on the use of copper wiring.

Still, given the previous rounds of funding, Democrats aren’t exactly lining up to ladle another $50 billion into the Trump administration’s hands — especially since antipathy toward the president runs hot in a party that is still on a high from its midterm victories.

Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), the ranking member on the Senate’s aviation subcommittee, responded to Duffy’s request with a social media post excoriating the GOP.

“There’s always been money for vanity projects. But none to fix our air traffic control systems?” the senator wrote. “Perhaps Trump should prioritize aviation safety over his pathetic Arch.”

All of that being said, the political trajectory of where things go from here is complicated.

Democrats don’t necessarily want to fork money over to Trump, but they also don’t want to be seen as standing in the way of necessary improvements to a vital element of national infrastructure.

Republicans want to support Trump and Duffy but are uneasy with a $50 billion figure that appears to have been arrived at by a back-of-the-envelope guess, at a point when even the Transportation secretary admitted the “root cause” of Friday’s outrage remained unclear.

“From the Democrats’ standpoint, vis-a-vis Duffy, I think they are going to haul him before Congress and hold him to account,” said Democratic strategist Mark Longabaugh.

Yet, Longabaugh added, “I do think Democrats will support efforts to make sure these kinds of things don’t happen. … There is a broad American consensus that we just haven’t taken care of our infrastructure in this country over a long period of time — and the air-traffic system is a big part of that.”

GOP strategist John Feehery said there was considerable pressure on the opposition party.

“I don’t think Democrats are going to want to be against FAA funding after what just happened,” Feehery said.

But he too acknowledged that the Trump-Duffy $50 billion request is “a lot of money.”

“I think it’s a good opening bid but I don’t think they are going to get all of it,” he said.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

As his time in Congress comes to an end, Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) is calling for Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to be replaced, describing his tenure as a “series of failures.” Cassidy was the deciding vote on Kennedy’s confirmation in committee last year.

After former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles was let go, Kennedy boasted that the Senate “no longer has any leverage over me” as Stephen Miller is now in the role.

CBS’s “Face the Nation” host Margaret Brennan asked Cassidy on Sunday to respond to these remarks.

“Well, first, he’s obviously trying to provide cover for failure as Secretary of Health and Human Services. He was supposed to be doing something positive on ultra-processed foods. That’s what MAHA moms wanted. There’s been minimal progress, and now we’ve lost our measles elimination status, and we have infants dying from measles,” said Cassidy.

“There is no logic. This is about covering a series of failures,” he added.

Cassidy, chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, voted in favor of sending Kennedy’s nomination to the floor last year, despite admitting to having many reservations over the nominee’s long history of questioning the safety and efficacy of vaccines.

Cassidy at the time said he received “serious commitments” from Kennedy and the Trump administration about vaccine policy and other issues. But Cassidy has since accused Kennedy of breaking those promises .

While expressing dismay over Kennedy’s actions as recently as August, saying it was “pretty evident” that the secretary had lied about his plans to change the vaccine schedule, Cassidy avoided expressing any regret over his decision.

The Sunday interview is the clearest indication from Cassidy of any buyer’s remorse when it comes to Kennedy

articles.summary: Presented by Google Public Sector. {beacon} Technology Technology The Big Story Nvidia scandal threatens dark cloud over Trump-Xi meeting The espionage and extramarital affair scandal surrounding Nvidia and its embattled founder, Jensen Huang, could throw a wrench into President Trump’s meeting this week with Chinese premier Xi Jinping. © Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Associated Press Trump…
articles.body:
Nvidia scandal threatens dark cloud over Trump-Xi meeting

The espionage and extramarital affair scandal surrounding Nvidia and its embattled founder, Jensen Huang , could throw a wrench into President Trump’s meeting this week with Chinese premier Xi Jinping.

© Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Associated Press

Trump is on his way to the Philippines and China this week for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit (ASEAN) and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), respectively, where artificial intelligence , trade and security issues are expected to come up in discussions.

The trip comes just days after Trump lost one of his closest allies in the technology world after Huang resigned from the company he founded more than 30 years ago.

Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told reporters he doubts Trump will bring up the scandal with Xi.

“Trump has stood by Huang personally, and my read is that he sees espionage as something major powers just do to each other,” Singleton said

articles.title: Follow the Leader: Democrats face party battle as divisions deepen
articles.summary: Democrats face internal divisions as Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer encounter resistance from members questioning their leadership and the party's direction.
articles.body: You can’t play follow the leader until you decide who you want to follow. That’s the conundrum facing House and Senate Democrats. Not all House Democrats are on board with promoting House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to Speaker. And Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is challenging Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for Majority Leader. "As of today, my position is no because that's what my constituents and my community is saying," said Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.) when asked if she backed Jeffries, "It's really about the process. We want a democratic process. And that's what we're really fighting for. It's not about one person." It may not be about one person. But no one is running against Jeffries. That’s why some Jeffries loyalists believe that House Democrats should endorse him for the Speakership by acclimation on Wednesday. SENATE DEM CHALLENGING SEN CHUCK SCHUMER FOR LEADERSHIP POST BACKS HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR HOUSE SPEAKER Rep.-elect Jessica Killin (D-Colo.) flipped a district from red to blue and endorses Jeffries. "He hasn't had the opportunity to work in the majority as a leader of our party yet and I want to give him that opportunity," said Killin. Yet nearby in in the Centennial State, progressive Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) isn’t in Jeffries camp. "Not yet," said Kiros when asked by yours truly if she would vote for Jeffries. "Ultimately this is about making sure that there is a democratic process in lieu of there not being multiple candidates." But reservations about Jeffries aren’t just coming from the left. Try the center. Rep.-elect Sam Forstag (D-MT) won a district in western Montana which President Trump carried by 11 points two years ago. Forstag. "I haven't committed my vote to anybody," said Forstag. "I'll be voting for whoever's going to actually help us modernize the way this place works." HAKEEM JEFFRIES FACES PROGRESSIVE HOLDOUTS BUT NO RIVAL AS HOUSE SPEAKER RACE TAKES SHAPE Before voters elected her to Congress, Killin toiled for multiple House Democrats as a chief of staff. She understands what Members must synthesize before supporting someone for leadership. "We have a wild and unwieldy freshman class. It's over 100 people. This is part of process," said Killin. "Each person needs to follow their own process on how we're electing leadership." House Republicans settled their leadership team last week, tapping Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) to serve as Minority Leader next year over current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.). Rep.-elect Chris Stigall (R-Mo.) may consider investing in tubs of popcorn as he watches leadership machinations across the aisle. "They're going to have one heck of a fight on their hands deciding who the voice of their party going forward is going to be," predicted Stigall. "If Team Jeffries can somehow manage to wrangle and herd those cats, it'll be a miracle, frankly." In the Senate, Van Hollen says midterm wins by Democrats in states which haven’t been in the Democratic column in years spurred his candidacy for Majority Leader. "We understand that this will be a competition," said Van Hollen. "I think it's important to give Senate Democrats a choice. That's what we just gave voters all over the country. A choice. They chose change." Schumer has led Senate Democrats for a decade. Van Hollen is nearly nine years younger than the 75-year-old Schumer — who turns 76 next week. Van Hollen has at least five senators or senators-elect who caucus with the Democrats who will support him. There are three senators who associate with the Democrats who won’t back Schumer as the next Majority Leader. "I've been open that I'm not voting for Sen. Schumer," said Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.). The revolt over Jeffries and Schumer reveals fractures between moderates and progressives. Plus old and new. Even Schumer’s hometown mayor sidestepped an opportunity to endorse the Brooklyn Democrat. "I care less about who it is and I care more about what they do with that power," said New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D). That says, Schumer has vocal supporters — including an ally from the Empire State. "This caucus is grateful for the hard work of Sen. Schumer. No one has put in the time and effort that anyone has put into this cycle than he did," said Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.). "That is why you will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position." "Chris Van Hollen is a great colleague," said Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.). "But I'm supporting Chuck Schumer." But even one Democrat aligned with Schumer says what gets done outweighs who does it. "I think no matter who is Leader, we're going to deliver on this agenda," said Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.). A small group of demonstrators cursed at Jeffries when he spoke at a Democrats’ conference in Colorado late last week. The protesters hollered about impeachment and called him a "f****** liar." Frication like that threatens to sidetrack Democrats. "There’s really a fight for the soul of the Democratic Party. Are they going to embrace these radical ideas?" asked Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.) on Fox. Some incoming progressives contend there’s no internal strife. "People try to say we're we're fractured as a party. In reality, we're all working on the same message," said Rep.-elect Donavan McKinney (D-Mich.). RACHEL MADDOW WELCOMES 'BIG FIGHT' BETWEEN SOCIALIST AND MODERATE DEMOCRATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS One Democrat said the internecine arguments are natural at this stage with Democrats just capturing big majorities. "I think a little bit of scrumming around inside the party is a good thing," said Rep.-elect Fred Wellman (D-Mo.) who defeated Rep. Ann Wagner (R-MO) in what had been an historically red district. "The wonderful thing about my party is we're more than happy to duke it out." Rep.-elect Eric Jones (D-Calif.) quibbles with the terminology characterizing Democratic disagreements. "I wouldn't go so far as to say ‘duke it out’ because those are fighting words," said Jones. "But there are definitely open conversations. They're pretty collegial. Pretty collaborative." But real differences exist. Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) says he opposes what he termed Van Hollen’s "strong, anti-Israel kinds of views." "I can't really think of what Van Hollen is known for. But he became like a progressive darling. But I don't see that he has a path to be leader," said Fetterman on Fox. Liberal Democrats believe Van Hollen is willing to enact progressive priorities – which may be controversial among centrist Democrats. "Sen. Van Hollen has been a long-time supporter of DC and DC statehood," said Washington, DC’s new non-voting delegate to the House, Del.-elect Robert White (D-DC). "I would get rid of the filibuster in order to get DC statehood." On Fox, Van Hollen said he wouldn’t end the filibuster "right out of the gate." But the Maryland Democrat added that the filibuster was an "undemocratic provision." Specifics matter in politics. They’ll matter if there’s a move to change the filibuster. Obliterating the filibuster might excite some progressives. But other Democrats may recoil. The same with Medicare for all. Progressives may embrace such a vote. But moderate Democrats who flipped red districts could abhor that prospect. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Those are the things which Democratic leaders must figure out. And when they do, only then will we know who is willing to follow them.

articles.title: Whip List: Schumer faces challenge from Van Hollen for Senate Democratic leader
articles.summary: Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, is facing a new leadership challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) after the big midterm wins by the party in November. Van Hollen, 67, is the progressive in the race, and his election would be a boost for the left. Upon declaring his…
articles.body:
Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, is facing a new leadership challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) after the big midterm wins by the party in November.

Van Hollen, 67, is the progressive in the race, and his election would be a boost for the left. Upon declaring his candidacy he was quickly endorsed by liberal Sen.-elects Peggy Flanagan (Minn.) and Abdul El-Sayed (Mich.).

Schumer, who turns 76 later this month, just led Democrats to sweeping victories in the midterm elections that saw the party gain eight Senate seats, with a ninth gain possible in Alaska.

While the age difference between the two men is not great, Van Hollen is pitching himself as the change candidate in the race. He supports ending the filibuster, is a backer of Medicare for All, and wants restrictions on U.S. military support for Israel.

The election is scheduled for Dec. 1, although Schumer’s allies are discussing moving the election earlier. It is a secret ballot race, but The Hill will be asking members about their votes and compiling the results here. A candidate needs 28 votes to win.

Here’s a look at who is backing which candidate in the race for Senate Democratic leader.

Last updated at 6:33 p.m. on Nov. 16 with Hirono, Hickenlooper.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisc.) : Baldwin has cited the party’s strong election performance as the reason to retain Schumer. “The Brewers just had a record season, and next year is not the time to change our management. The same is true in the Senate,” she said in a statement.

Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) : Brown was recruited by Schumer to fun for his old seat in Ohio and prevailed, giving a victory to the Democratic leader. He’s in turning backing Schumer.

Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) : “Leader Schumer was instrumental in Democrats flipping eight — soon to be nine — Senate seats and securing a historic majority,” Cortez Masto wrote on X.

Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) : Fetterman has strongly supported Schumer throughout his tenure in the Senate and will continue to do so. In a Nov. 14 Fox News interview, Fetterman said Van Hollen’s position on Israel could cause him to leave the Democratic Party if the Maryland senator was elected as majority leader.

Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) : Gallego said that while he’s had his differences with Schumer, he still supports the New Yorker’s leadership. “It’s time for us to unify, we are going to work together as a caucus and put a plan together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think, you know, we have the person who’s going to lead us there.”

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.): Gillibrand credited Schumer for the sweeping Democratic victories in the 2026 midterms, saying the blue wave wasn’t “created by magic.”

Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) : Hirono on Monday said she has a long history with Van Hollen and respects him a lot. But she said she also has a long history with Schumer. “I’m supporting Chuck because of the long history I have with Chuck,” she said.

Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) : “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” he said in a statement.

Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) : Schatz is poised to become the next Senate Democratic whip in January. He released a statement endorsing Schumer for leader.

Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) : Schumer would vote for himself.

Senators publicly backing Van Hollen (5)

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) : El-Sayed was the first to explicitly back Van Hollen, before Van Hollen had even announced a bid for Leader. He had endorsed the Maryland senator months earlier during the campaign, repeatedly saying he’d be “amazing” at the job and even introducing Van Hollen at a rally as “the next Senate majority leader.”

Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) : Flanagan called in a social media post for “new voices in our leadership” and pledged her support for Van Hollen on Nov. 13 .

Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) : Merkley became one of a few early supporters of Van Hollen’s bid, announcing on social media last week that he was supporting Van Hollen because “politics as usual is unacceptable.”

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) : Sanders also committed his vote to Van Hollen early, saying he would not support Schumer’s leadership and then pledging support for Van Hollen shortly thereafter.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) : Van Hollen would vote for himself

Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.) : Andrews, who won a stunning upset over a Republican incumbent in deep-red South Carolina, has pledged not to support Schumer, saying she wants “a generational change” in leadership. But she has yet to give her support to Van Hollen or anyone else. Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.)

Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) : Booker is a member of Democratic leadership but has not publicly supported either candidate.

Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D-Miss.) : Reports have said Schumer recruited Colom to run, but Colom pushed back on that characterization, saying it was the people of Mississippi that deserved credit for his success. Colom did not commit to voting for or against Schumer at that point, saying “I got to know my options.”

Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) : Coons and Kim have called for a caucus debate over leadership.

Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.): Hamilton is the first Democratic senator from Kansas in nearly a century, and said he would not back Schumer for leader during his campaign, calling the Democratic leader “ a polarizing figure .” A centrist representing what has been a red state, Hamilton now faces a decision between Schumer and a more liberal alternative.

Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) : Hickenlooper said Monday that Schumer deserves credit for helping to flip nine Republican Senate seats in the midterm election — assuming the Alaska race is called for Democrats. “Obviously there are some things Chuck does very well. We just flipped nine Senate seats. It’s hard to condemn a man who’s just done one of the primary goals of his job, [which] is to deliver that,” he said. Hickenlooper said his “best case” expectation heading into Election Day was that Democrats would pick up five seats. Even so, Hickenlooper said it’s healthy “from time to time to take a look at how the caucus functions.

Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine): Jackson has called for new leadership but hasn’t endorsed Van Hollen. Just before Election Day, Jackson said he would not support Schumer. “I told Schumer that I’m going to, you know, support somebody else,” Jackson told reporters. “So it’s no different now.” Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.)

Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) : Along with Coons, Kim has called for a caucus debate over leadership.

Sen.-elect Chris Pappas (D-N.H.): Pappas has called for new leadership but has not endorsed Van Hollen over Schumer.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) : She has called for change but hasn’t endorsed either candidate.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) : A key Senate progressive, Warren has worked closely with Schumer in the past and is someone to watch.

Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.): Before Van Hollen announced his candidacy, Welch told NBC 5 Democrats “absolutely are committed to change,” but didn’t rule out supporting Schumer.

This list will be updated as more senators make their positions known. Please e-mail us with any tips at edt-grp@thehill.com

articles.body:
Rep.-elect Fred Wellman (D-Mo.) accused Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth of committing “war crimes” during his tenure as head of the Pentagon.

“Actually, I believe he’s committed crimes,” Wellman said during an appearance on MS NOW . “And let’s be very clear: we’re not at war with anyone in South America at this point. The boats that we are striking in the Pacific and in the Caribbean, who are they? As far as we’re being told, they’re drug boats.”

“But I’m not sure if I remember a time in American history where we’re allowed to execute people simply for the accusation of a crime,” he continued. “The fact is, we have been striking these boats. We’ve killed hundreds of people with little or no explanation.”

Wellman noted his experience as a retired Army officer, where he served for 22 years and was deployed to combat four times, saying, “we owe it to those troops who are pulling those triggers to know exactly what’s going on because they’re being asked to kill people.”

“That responsibility is a very serious one and I don’t believe that Pete Hegseth or frankly Donald Trump take that at all seriously,” he concluded. “So I’m not just saying it’s war crimes. I think it’s fair to say it’s straight up crimes. It’s murder.”

Earlier in the interview, Wellman also revealed he has known Hegseth for 15 years but disliked the defense secretary for “about 14.99 of those years.”

The incoming lawmaker floated investigating the Defense Department for high-profile removals Hegseth conducted – including reports that he denied promotions to military members who supported the COVID vaccine.

Hegseth was nearly impeached last week after outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced eight articles of impeachment against him. The impeachment efforts accused Hegseth of violating the Constitution and other laws during U.S. military operations in Yemen, Iran, the Caribbean and the Eastern Pacific.

Massie won’t be returning to the lower chamber as he lost reelection to Trump-backed Rep.-elect Ed Gallerein (R-Ky.) though House Democrats have signalled plans to conduct greater oversight into Hegseth and the Defense Department.

“When Democrats take the majority in the 120th Congress, we will hold Secretary Hegseth accountable for his illegal actions,” Rep. Betty McCollum (D-Minn.), top Democrat of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, previously said in a statement.

articles.body: Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., announced Monday night that he is running for governor of Kentucky in an attempt to flip the governor’s mansion from blue to red in 2027. The Republican congressman’s announcement comes on the heels this month’s blue tsunami that swept Democrats into control of both chambers of Congress. Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, who is term limited, has led Kentucky since 2019, though voters backed Republicans for statewide positions in the midterm elections. Comer announced his candidacy in a tele-town hall, where he took questions from callers. While answering one of the questions, the congressman sought to create some distance from President Donald Trump. “I think that some of the things the president has tried to do on the national level had good intentions, but there are always unintended consequences,” said Comer, who like many House Republicans aligned himself with Trump over the years. Comer was first elected to Congress in 2016. He currently serves as chair of the House Oversight Committee, which oversaw Congress’ probe into Jeffrey Epstein. Kentucky is one of the few states to have off-year elections for governor — the others are Louisiana and Mississippi. The 2027 election could be an early test of how durable the blue wave will prove one year out from the midterm elections — and a year before the 2028 presidential election. Trump won Kentucky by more than 30 percentage points in 2024, and Comer won re-election this year by an even wider margin, defeating his Democratic opponent by more than 35 points. Comer is the biggest name to jump into the race on the GOP side. Three other Republicans have declared their intentions to run, including former reality TV contestant Charles “Bruiser” Martin and Rick Hardin, a state attorney. On the Democratic side, Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former Beshear senior adviser Rocky Adkins have said they are running. Kentucky will hold its primaries on May 18.

articles.title: Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does data show?
articles.summary: Votes are still being counted in the Alaska Senate race, with Democrat Mary Peltola ahead of Republican incumbent Senator Dan S Sullivan.
articles.body:
Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.

This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".

US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election.

But with 97% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.

Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.

BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.

The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.

This calls into question claims that Republican voters may have been confused about which Sullivan they were voting for.

How did two Dan Sullivans end up in the race?

Republican Dan S Sullivan has held the US Senate seat in Alaska since 2015 and was running for his third term.

Daniel J Sullivan Jr - a retired school teacher from a remote fishing village in Alaska - entered the race in May and has run a low-key campaign.

A New York Times story published the week before Election Day claimed that Democratic operatives with links to the Peltola campaign had tried to recruit "spoiler" candidates in the Senate race, including Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

The report said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.

Peltola has denied all knowledge of the alleged "scheme" and Sullivan Jr has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.

President Trump has posted multiple times on Truth Social since the election, claiming that the race has been "rigged".

But experts note it's not an illegal tactic, if it was employed.

"There is nothing to prevent a campaign from recruiting someone else to run, even if for political reasons," said Joshua Douglas, an election law expert at the University of Kentucky.

Voters in Alaska select their first choice candidate, followed by options to rank up to four other candidates in order of preference.

"There is no specific law preventing people with the same name running, but many states have laws or regulations about how names appear on the ballot. One of those regulations was used in Alaska" said Ruth Greenwood, director of the election law clinic at Harvard Law School.

On Alaskans' ballots the two Sullivans were listed as:

Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent

There was a second registered Republican candidate, Gerald Heikes - who was also allegedly recruited into the race according to The New York Times.

As of Monday, Peltola holds 49.94% of the vote.

In the event that Peltola were not to clear 50%, officials eliminate the candidate in last place and reallocate those ballots to the voters' next choices. This process continues until two candidates remain, with one clearing the 50% hurdle.

Daniel J Sullivan Jr is the listed candidate in last place with 1.65% of the vote.

What does ranked-choice voting data show so far?

Senator Dan S Sullivan and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.

Trump said last week: "Anybody that voted for that second Dan Sullivan, the fake Dan Sullivan, was supposed to be a vote for the real Dan Sullivan".

Of the ballots analysed by BBC Verify that ranked Daniel J Sullivan Jr first, 38% of them recorded no valid second choice.

We do not know how many of these voters may have thought they had voted for the Senator Dan S Sullivan and then not ranked any other candidates.

A further 29% of Daniel J Sullivan Jr voters ranked the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola second, almost double the 15% that ranked the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan as second.

"The likelihood that any confusion might play a significant role is diminished in Alaska," Richard Pildes, a professor of constitutional law at New York University, argues, "because any voter who was unsure which Dan Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for could rank them first and second."

Additional reporting by Wesley Stephenson and Daniel Wainwright

articles.title: Biden library nears site decision as fundraising trails ambitions: report
articles.summary: Joe Biden’s presidential library foundation is reportedly nearing a Delaware site decision after securing multimillion-dollar donations in 2026.
articles.body: Former President Joe Biden’s presidential library foundation is reportedly closing in on a location in Delaware, even as its fundraising efforts continue to fall short of expectations. Despite receiving several multimillion-dollar gifts in 2026, the Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation is working to overcome a difficult fundraising start, following a roughly $600,000 deficit in 2025, according to filings reported by CBS News. The foundation reportedly raised $1.5 million in 2025 but spent $2.1 million. An official told the outlet that the organization was not actively soliciting donations that year, characterizing it instead as a "building and infrastructure year." The expenses, which were partly covered by contributions from Biden’s presidential inaugural committee and individual donors, primarily went toward staff, consultants and legal fees. Roughly $250,000 was specifically paid to consultants tasked with laying the groundwork for the foundation’s fundraising operation, the outlet said. EX-DEM FUNDRAISER TORCHES BIDEN AS BOOK LAUNCH IMPLODES: 'NO ONE WANTS TO READ' This year, the foundation secured two $5 million gifts among its donations, according to reports. CBS News noted that the foundation is now seeking to capitalize on the post-midterm political climate, as wealthy Democrats reportedly poured money into campaigns that helped fuel sweeping victories for the party. Despite this year's fundraising recoveries, some of Biden’s close allies have reportedly criticized Democratic donors for failing to proactively offer support for his library. Biden has "never been a good fundraiser, even when he was in the Senate," one source said. His wife Jill is also expected to help with fundraising as Biden undergoes treatment for prostate cancer. JOE BIDEN SAYS CANCER SLOWED HIM DOWN, LIMITING MEMOIR PROMOTION TOUR The foundation has also expanded its board with five new members, bringing in a mix of diplomatic, business and nonprofit experience as it seeks to strengthen its fundraising efforts, according to reports. The reported additions include Elizabeth Frawley Bagley, Biden’s former ambassador to Brazil; Bijan Sabet, a venture capitalist and former ambassador to the Czech Republic; event planner Bryan Rafanelli; Wilmington nonprofit leader Logan Herring; and Annie Tomasini, a former White House deputy chief of staff. OBAMA CENTER ISN'T A TRADITIONAL PRESIDENTIAL LIBRARY. CRITICS SAY IT'S AN ACTIVISM CENTER. The library’s fundraising performance could offer a window into Biden’s standing within the Democratic Party and the extent to which wealthy donors are still willing to contribute to preserving his political legacy. His support among some donors has been strained by frustrations with his presidency and his decision to pardon his son, Hunter. As Biden works to build financial support for the project, the foundation’s fundraising total still pales in comparison with that of President Donald Trump’s presidential library foundation, which has already secured tens of millions of dollars. articles.title: Ro Khanna pitches $1,700 checks for Americans to offset Iran war costs: 'A chance to deliver'
articles.summary: Rep. Ro Khanna proposed a $1,700 refund check for every American family to cover higher gas, food and electricity bills tied to the war in Iran.
articles.body: Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., on Monday proposed giving every American family a $1,700 refund check to offset higher costs driven by the war in Iran. Khanna, a frequent critic of President Donald Trump's war in the Middle East, said the checks would be sent to every American family to reimburse them for the higher gas, food and electricity prices sparked by the conflict and resulting disruptions to oil transport routes. The congressman said Democrats "have a chance to deliver" following their sweeping midterm victories earlier this month, urging the House and Senate to approve the payments in January. "I want to give every American family a $1,700 check to make them whole for the war in Iran," Khanna said in a video posted to X. RO KHANNA REJECTS WARNINGS THAT TRUMP ADMIN INVESTIGATIONS COULD DERAIL DEMOCRATS' AFFORDABILITY AGENDA "This is to cover their higher gas prices, their higher food prices, their higher electricity bills. Now Democrats have a chance to deliver. The first week in January, the House and Senate must pass a $1,700 refund check to Americans. Let’s put it on Donald Trump’s desk," he continued. Khanna had previously urged Congress to block all funding for the war. Khanna also introduced legislation in September that would redirect certain unused Pentagon funds to compensate taxpayers and dependents for the economic costs of the war. The bill does not specify a $1,700 payment and has not advanced beyond the committee referral stage. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, estimated last month that the conflict in Iran had cost the average American household about $2,000, adding up to $265 billion nationwide. His estimate included higher energy costs, borrowing costs and military expenditures. VOTERS HAVE A BLUNT MESSAGE FOR TRUMP ABOUT HIS IDEA TO DOLE OUT $5,000 CHECKS Gas prices soared after the war began in February, with the national average rising above $4 per gallon before declining in recent weeks. The average was $3.81 per gallon as of Monday, about 75 cents more than a year ago, according to AAA. Diesel averaged nearly $6 per gallon, about $2.23 more than a year earlier. Trump has repeatedly argued that higher prices are worth it to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon, although the president, Vice President JD Vance and other Republican leaders have acknowledged that the party's midterm losses were at least partially due to Americans' frustrations about higher prices. Before the midterms, the president promised a $5,000 "Trump dividend" check to every adult U.S. citizen if the Republican Party retained control of the House and Senate, but Republicans lost control of both chambers. TRUMP’S $5K CHECKS COULD JOIN STACK OF PAST UNFULFILLED PROMISES, FORMER CONGRESS BUDGET CHIEF WARNS Several GOP leaders expressed skepticism about Trump's plan, pointing to concerns over the escalating national debt, potential inflationary pressures and the need for congressional approval. It remains unclear if Khanna's proposal will receive the same pushback from Democrats. articles.title: Vance says there’s ‘no daylight’ between him and Trump on the war in Iran
articles.summary: JD Vance on Monday said he and President Donald Trump are totally aligned on the war in Iran after the vice president this month attributed Republicans’ electoral beatdown in the midterm elections to voter frustrations with the conflict.
articles.body: JD Vance on Monday said he and President Donald Trump are totally aligned on the war in Iran after the vice president this month attributed Republicans’ electoral beatdown in the midterm elections to voter frustrations with the conflict. “There’s no daylight, Laura,” Vance told Fox News host Laura Ingraham in his first TV interview since the midterms. “And I think there’s no daylight between the president or any other senior member of the administration. Now, politically, yes, and I think the president himself has absolutely said this as well, there was a political cost: the higher gas prices, the higher energy prices.” Vance, a potential 2028 presidential contender, also argued that other factors have also contributed to higher fuel prices, including what he described as a lack of investment in American energy infrastructure in recent decades. It was part of a broader theme he echoed throughout the interview, doubling down on what he dubbed “economic nationalism,” and calling to re-shore factories as a response to the election results. “Now we got shellacked, of course we did, and I do think that we have to take messages from that,” Vance said. “But the message that we have to take from that is that the American people want prosperity, they want freedom, they want sovereignty within their own country, and they want us to do more of the good things that we’ve done, and they also want us to recognize that there is some economic pain out there in the United States of America.” “But the way that you deal with that economic pain, it’s not by opening the border, it’s not by giving up on American sovereignty, and it’s sure as hell not by shipping more American factories and more American jobs overseas,” he continued. “It’s doubling down on economic nationalism and bringing prosperity to the homeland.” Immediately after Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections — the party’s strongest electoral performance since just after the Watergate scandal — Vance took to X to write: “The reason we lost is the war,” adding that Trump himself had made similar remarks. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he wrote on X, seemingly to Republicans who have more forcefully backed the war. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” Trump later told reporters he thought Vance’s analysis was correct, but added that his vice president “should have made one other statement … If you had it to do again, would you do it again? The answer is yes.” Those remarks preceded the president last week announcing he was taking Vance off of Iran peace negotiations, asking him to instead redouble his focus on alleged government benefits fraud. In his Fox News interview, Vance confidently pledged that the administration is “not going to allow” the war to become “even a two-year commitment.” Trump and senior administration officials said at the onset of the conflict, which began Feb. 28, that it would be wrapped up within a matter of weeks. “But my prediction, Laura, is that whatever the president ultimately decides to do, there are going to be people who demand more, who want the war to go on indefinitely, and what I feel quite confident about the president of the United States, and again, there’s no daylight here, is that whatever he ultimately decides to do, however he ultimately decides to bring the conflict to a close, he is not going to let this become a forever war,” Vance said. “And the people who want it to become a forever war, they can attack me all they want to because we signed up to not do this, we told the American people we would do no more forever wars.” “Yes, the president felt he had to destroy the nuclear program, and yes, the Iranian nuclear program is a threat to the United States of America,” Vance continued. “But we are not going to allow this to become a 10- or 15-year commitment, or frankly, even a two-year commitment.” The vice president said he hasn’t made up his mind on running for president in 2028 but said a decision will come “sometime next year.” “When I make a decision, Laura, I will be all in on whatever that decision is,” he said. On the scandal that has engulfed former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Vance said the core issue at play isn’t whether he had a relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset — which Vance said the administration was not sure of — but was about reindustrializing the U.S., in this case so that the supply chain of the advanced chips needed to fuel the AI boom is more fully contained domestically. “The main issue is we need to reindustrialize the country and protect our critical technology and our critical infrastructure,” he said. “And the only way to do that is to build more of it in the United States of America and prevent it from falling into the wrong hands.” Responding to a question about Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., who Vance frequently clashed with on the campaign trail, the vice president expressed hope the two of them and other newly elected Democrats could work together. “So, I hope Democrats actually try to govern on what they ran on. Because if you look at what they ran on, what do they talk about? Reindustrializing America, lowering energy costs for Americans,” he said. “They ran on a lot of the themes that Donald Trump ran on in 2024. Let’s work together.” Ingraham pressed Vance on the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide ground stop on Friday that stranded hundreds of thousands of passengers after a router issue derailed air traffic control communications as well as a series of other tech outages in recent days. Vance echoed other administration officials in requesting new funding from Congress to modernize the air traffic control system while seeking to assure viewers that these problems were not building up to some larger crisis. “Yeah, I’ve had a lot of my friends reach out and say, ‘Should we be preparing to build a bunker or to stock up on food and water?’ And my answer to that is no,” Vance said after Ingraham pointed to European governments recently pushing citizens to ramp up their emergency preparedness. “We do not see some crisis coming down, but you have to be prepared for everything. And what we want to do is make sure that we prevent the worst outcomes, but we’re also prepared for the worst outcomes.”
